'providedIn: "root"' creates a singleton instance shared across the entire application, whereas a lazy-loaded component's 'providers' array creates a new instance scoped strictly to that lazy-loaded injector hierarchy and its children
There is no difference in runtime behavior; both register the service in the root application injector
questions.correctAnswer: 'providedIn: "root"' creates a singleton instance shared across the entire application, whereas a lazy-loaded component's 'providers' array creates a new instance scoped strictly to that lazy-loaded injector hierarchy and its children
questions.explanation: Services specified in 'providedIn: root' are application-wide singletons. Conversely, declaring a service in a component's 'providers' array creates a distinct injector instance scoped to that component tree, shadowing any root provider and destroying the service instance when the component is destroyed.
questions.hint: Consider hierarchical injectors and scoping boundaries.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Hierarchical Injector Scoping
questions.interviewTip: Expect this question to test whether developers understand memory leaks and state sharing bugs caused by incorrect service scoping in lazy-loaded modules.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q3] What happens when an Angular component using OnPush change detection strategy mutates a property of an input @Input object directly without replacing the reference?
options: The view updates immediately because Angular zones intercept all property mutations.
Angular automatically clones the object and triggers a change detection cycle.
TypeScript compiler throws a type error preventing direct mutations on input properties.
The view is not updated because OnPush only checks reference changes on @Input properties.
questions.correctAnswer: The view is not updated because OnPush only checks reference changes on @Input properties.
questions.explanation: With OnPush change detection, Angular relies on shallow reference comparison (Object.is) for @Input properties. Mutating internal properties of an object reference rather than assigning a new object instance will bypass change detection unless explicitly marked with ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck().
questions.hint: Think about reference equality checks versus deep object observation in change detection.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular OnPush Change Detection and Object Reference Mutation
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify a deep understanding of Angular's rendering optimizations and the limitations of reference-based change detection strategies.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q4] When developing custom Angular form validators that execute asynchronously, what is the exact consequence of failing to return an observable that completes?
options: The form control status remains permanently stuck in 'PENDING', preventing the form from ever becoming valid or dirty-submittable.
Angular automatically times out the observable after 5 seconds and marks the control as invalid.
An unhandled memory leak occurs, but the form validation proceeds synchronously with cached values.
The async validator is treated as a synchronous validator, forcing immediate execution.
questions.correctAnswer: The form control status remains permanently stuck in 'PENDING', preventing the form from ever becoming valid or dirty-submittable.
questions.explanation: Angular's AbstractControl watches the status of async validators by subscribing to the returned observable. If the observable does not emit and complete (common with HttpClient gets which auto-complete, but fatal with subjects or incomplete streams), the control status permanently remains 'PENDING'.
questions.hint: Consider how Reactive Forms determine when validation finishes by listening to observable completion or emission.
questions.relatedConcept: Reactive Forms Async Validators and Stream Completion
questions.interviewTip: This question screens candidates for real-world production experience with Reactive Forms and RxJS stream lifecycles.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q5] How does Angular's experimental zoneless change detection mechanism (utilizing `provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection`) fundamentally manage asynchronous operations and trigger view refreshes compared to Zone.js?
options: It relies on RxJS scheduler notifications emitted exclusively by `HttpClient` and `Router` event streams to flag dirty components.
It hooks directly into native browser primitives like `requestAnimationFrame` and microtask queues to schedule component tree re-renders.
It requires developers to manually call `ChangeDetectorRef.detectChanges()` within every asynchronous callback since automatic monkey-patching is entirely removed.
It intercepts primitive JavaScript runtime hooks via V8-specific APIs to track variable mutations across component boundaries.
questions.correctAnswer: It hooks directly into native browser primitives like `requestAnimationFrame` and microtask queues to schedule component tree re-renders.
questions.explanation: Zoneless change detection in Angular leverages standard browser APIs, signals, and asynchronous primitives (such as Promises, microtasks, and `requestAnimationFrame`) to notify the framework when state changes might have occurred, eliminating the performance overhead and monkey-patching of Zone.js.
questions.hint: Think about what triggers state synchronization when Zone.js is completely absent.
questions.relatedConcept: Zoneless Change Detection and RxJS/Signals Integration
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask about zoneless architecture to gauge your understanding of modern Angular performance optimization and the shift away from Zone.js dependency.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q6] When building custom structural directives in Angular using the new microsyntax parser introduced alongside control flow blocks (`@if`, `@for`), what is the primary role of `ViewContainerRef` combined with `TemplateRef` in performance optimization?
options: They automatically memoize template rendering results to bypass HTML string serialization during SSR.
They cache compiled AST structures within the JIT compiler to speed up dynamic template factories.
They allow precise, lazy instantiation and destruction of DOM nodes in-memory without incurring full component lifecycle re-evaluations.
They force synchronous layout recalculations to prevent layout thrashing during animation sequences.
questions.correctAnswer: They allow precise, lazy instantiation and destruction of DOM nodes in-memory without incurring full component lifecycle re-evaluations.
questions.explanation: `ViewContainerRef` and `TemplateRef` allow structural directives to explicitly instantiate, attach, move, or destroy embedded views on-demand, optimizing DOM insertion and memory usage for conditional or repeating content.
questions.hint: Consider how DOM elements are dynamically added and removed granularly.
questions.relatedConcept: Structural Directives and ViewContainerRef Lifecycle
questions.interviewTip: This tests low-level rendering mechanics and DOM manipulation strategies beyond basic component bindings.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q7] When developing a complex Angular application utilizing Zone.js, what is the precise primary consequence of executing code inside `NgZone.runOutsideAngular` when performance tuning an intensive frequent event listener like `mousemove`?
options: It completely unsubscribes the underlying DOM event listener from bubbling and stops the event propagation loop in the browser.
It detaches the component from the root injector context, making it incapable of injecting services or receiving dependency injection tokens.
It marks the component and all its parent components as 'Dirty' within the Ivy runtime, bypassing standard OnPush checks.
It prevents every 'mousemove' event emission from triggering an unnecessary global change detection cycle across the component tree, drastically reducing CPU overhead.
questions.correctAnswer: It prevents every 'mousemove' event emission from triggering an unnecessary global change detection cycle across the component tree, drastically reducing CPU overhead.
questions.explanation: Code executed inside `runOutsideAngular` runs outside the Angular Zone. Therefore, asynchronous operations or events triggered within that block do not notify Zone.js, preventing it from automatically scheduling a global change detection check. This is crucial for high-frequency events like scroll, mousemove, or requestAnimationFrame to prevent UI jank.
questions.hint: Consider how Zone.js intercepts browser macro and microtasks to schedule updates.
questions.relatedConcept: Zone.js performance optimization and NgZone execution contexts
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers love asking this to see if candidates understand how Angular ties DOM event listeners to change detection cycles and how to avoid performance bottlenecks.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q8] In Angular 16+ reactive programming paradigms, what distinguishes the execution behavior of the new `toSignal()` conversion function when unwrap/read operations occur outside of an active reactive context (like an injection context or computed function)?
options: It throws a runtime error unless an explicit `initialValue` is supplied or it is evaluated within an injection context.
It automatically creates a persistent subscription that remains active for the lifetime of the application without ever unsubscribing.
It converts the observable into a cold observable that executes its source producer lazily upon every read.
It forces the dependency injection container to immediately evaluate and memoize the stream's final emitted value.
questions.correctAnswer: It throws a runtime error unless an explicit `initialValue` is supplied or it is evaluated within an injection context.
questions.explanation: The `toSignal()` utility implicitly creates a subscription to the source Observable. If called outside an injection context (like a service constructor property initializer), Angular requires either an `initialValue` option or the `requireSync: true` flag to handle the synchronous gap before the first emission, otherwise, it throws a runtime error because it cannot register cleanup or obtain an injector.
questions.hint: Think about how signals bridge RxJS observables and how lifecycle/injection contexts manage subscriptions safely.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Signals toSignal() operator and injection context requirements
questions.codeSnippet: const mySignal = toSignal(myObservable$, { initialValue: 0 });
questions.interviewTip: Expect this question when assessing modern Angular migration strategies from RxJS to Signals, focusing on edge cases in initialization.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q9] When utilizing the Angular AsyncPipe with an Observable that emits frequently inside a high-throughput NgZone-disabled context (runOutsideAngular), how does the change detection cycle interact with the subscription cleanup if the host component is destroyed?
options: The subscription remains active unless explicitly torn down via takeUntil or destroy$ because runOutsideAngular prevents automatic garbage collection of observables.
AsyncPipe automatically unsubscribes on component destruction, and its internal change detector reference is detached from the global tree when view destruction runs.
Memory leaks occur because AsyncPipe retains a strong reference to the NgZone instance even after component destruction.
The subscription is cleaned up only when the parent module is unloaded from the application injector hierarchy.
questions.correctAnswer: AsyncPipe automatically unsubscribes on component destruction, and its internal change detector reference is detached from the global tree when view destruction runs.
questions.explanation: The AsyncPipe internally manages the subscription lifecycle. When the component's view is destroyed, the pipe's ngOnDestroy method executes, unsubscribing from the source observable and releasing any held references, regardless of whether emissions occur inside or outside NgZone.
questions.hint: Think about the lifecycle hooks implemented internally by built-in pipes like AsyncPipe.
questions.relatedConcept: AsyncPipe lifecycle management and view destruction
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to test deep knowledge of built-in directive internals and whether developers blindly add manual takeUntil operators when AsyncPipe already handles cleanup.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q10] What is the primary architectural mechanism responsible for memory retention when a custom structural directive dynamically instantiates views via ViewContainerRef.createEmbeddedView() and the component is subsequently destroyed?
options: Angular automatically garbage collects all embedded views synchronously via finalizers once the host element loses its renderer attachment.
The Ivy runtime automatically serializes embedded views into string templates, moving them out of heap memory entirely.

Embedded views created dynamically retain references to their originating injector and template nodes; if not explicitly cleared from the ViewContainerRef or if host bindings keep element references alive, the embedded view nodes can cause DOM detachment memory leaks.
Dynamic embedded views maintain a strong circular reference to the root ApplicationRef, preventing the entire application from being garbage collected.
questions.correctAnswer: Embedded views created dynamically retain references to their originating injector and template nodes; if not explicitly cleared from the ViewContainerRef or if host bindings keep element references alive, the embedded view nodes can cause DOM detachment memory leaks.
questions.explanation: When views are manually created via ViewContainerRef, they are attached to the view tree. If the parent component is destroyed, Angular destroys child views, but references can linger if detached views hold onto injector states or if asynchronous operations maintain closures over the template context.
questions.hint: Consider how dynamic view containers tie template nodes to specific component injectors.
questions.relatedConcept: ViewContainerRef memory management and dynamic view destruction
questions.interviewTip: Useful for evaluating advanced frontend engineering skills regarding manual DOM manipulation, garbage collection hazards, and proper resource disposal in custom structural directives.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q11] In Angular, when using an `AsyncPipe` inside a component template to subscribe to a `BehaviorSubject`, what precise timing mechanism and lifecycle consideration prevents memory leaks and ensures safe cleanup during component destruction?
options: The AsyncPipe utilizes Zone.js microtask queues to hold references; if the BehaviorSubject is not completed manually in ngOnDestroy, the root injector retains the subscription indefinitely.
The AsyncPipe creates an independent internal subscription that persists across component re-creations unless bound using structural directives like *ngIf with safe navigation operators.
The AsyncPipe does not handle unsubscription automatically; instead, it relies on the garbage collector, requiring developers to invoke unsubscribe() in ngOnDestroy to avoid dangling references.

The AsyncPipe automatically subscribes on component initialization and explicitly manages unsubscription when the component instance is destroyed, meaning manual unsubscription is unnecessary for pipes bound in the template.
questions.correctAnswer: The AsyncPipe automatically subscribes on component initialization and explicitly manages unsubscription when the component instance is destroyed, meaning manual unsubscription is unnecessary for pipes bound in the template.
questions.explanation: The AsyncPipe internally subscribes to the Observable during instantiation and automatically unsubscribes when the component or the view containing the binding is destroyed, preventing memory leaks without requiring explicit cleanup code in ngOnDestroy.
questions.hint: Think about what Angular's built-in AsyncPipe does under the hood when a view is destroyed.
questions.relatedConcept: AsyncPipe lifecycle management and automatic unsubscription
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers love asking about subscription management to see if candidates understand how AsyncPipe simplifies memory handling compared to manual subscriptions.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q12] What is the execution order and change detection impact when a Signal is updated inside an Effect within an Angular component that utilizes zoneless change detection (`provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()`)?
options: Angular throws a runtime error preventing infinite loops (e.g., detecting cyclic writes within reactive graph dependencies), because signals cannot be written to synchronously inside an effect computation phase.
The effect executes continuously in a tight synchronous loop until the browser crashes due to a maximum call stack exceeded error.
Zoneless change detection catches the modification, defers the update to the next microtask, and increments the count exactly once without triggering reactive errors.
The effect updates the signal only once because Angular effects are designed with built-in debouncing mechanisms that ignore inner synchronous writes.
questions.correctAnswer: Angular throws a runtime error preventing infinite loops (e.g., detecting cyclic writes within reactive graph dependencies), because signals cannot be written to synchronously inside an effect computation phase.
questions.explanation: Angular's reactive system explicitly disallows writing to signals inside an `effect()` to prevent infinite loops and unpredictable state cycles. Attempting to update a signal synchronously inside its own dependent effect throws a runtime error.
questions.hint: Consider the safety checks Angular implements to prevent infinite reactivity loops inside effects.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Signals reactive graph constraints and effect write restrictions
questions.interviewTip: This tests deep knowledge of Angular's new Signals architecture, specifically the guardrails against side-effect cascades and cyclic updates.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q13] When developing an Angular application using Zone.js, what does a persistent 'ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError' during development most fundamentally imply about the component lifecycle?
options: The asynchronous event loop is blocked by an infinite RxJS observable pipe executing continuously in the background.
A binding or property was mutated during or after the view verification phase, causing a state drift between the model and the DOM before the next change detection cycle began.
Two competing child components are writing to the same parent Input decorator without emitting a corresponding Output event.
The Angular compiler detected a circular dependency in the dependency injection container while resolving token metadata.
questions.correctAnswer: A binding or property was mutated during or after the view verification phase, causing a state drift between the model and the DOM before the next change detection cycle began.
questions.explanation: Angular's development-mode change detection runs a secondary verification pass immediately after checking a component tree's views to ensure no bindings changed during the check. If a lifecycle hook (like ngAfterViewChecked) mutates a property bound in the template, the recorded value differs from the newly evaluated value, triggering the ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError.
questions.hint: Think about what phase runs after view rendering and what happens if a component updates its own bound properties during that phase.
questions.relatedConcept: ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError diagnostic analysis in Angular Zone.js lifecycle
questions.interviewTip: Interweaves Angular lifecycle execution order with the internal mechanics of change detection verification passes.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q14] An Angular application exhibits silent subscription leaks and UI components failing to update after router navigation, even though local component variables are assigned correctly inside an injected service. What does this symptom pattern suggest about the service architecture?
options: The service is missing the @Optional decorator, causing the dependency injector to return undefined instances on route changes.
The Observable is cold and multicasted improperly, causing each route navigation to instantiate a fresh execution thread.
The service is provided in 'root' (a singleton), maintaining global state and subscriptions across component destructions without proper unsubscription or lifecycle teardown.
The Ivy renderer has optimized out change detection for services marked with providedIn: 'root'.
questions.correctAnswer: The service is provided in 'root' (a singleton), maintaining global state and subscriptions across component destructions without proper unsubscription or lifecycle teardown.
questions.explanation: Services provided in 'root' have a singleton lifetime that outlives individual component lifecycles and router navigation events. If components subscribe to observables or retain references without unsubscribing when destroyed, or if the service logic relies on component lifecycle assumptions, state corruption and memory leaks ensue.
questions.hint: Consider the lifecycle scope of root-provided services versus component-scoped services during router transitions.
questions.relatedConcept: Root injector singleton lifetime management and reactive subscription lifecycle leaks
questions.interviewTip: Evaluates the candidate's understanding of DI scopes, singleton lifecycles, and memory management in Angular applications.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q15] When utilizing `ViewContainerRef.createEmbeddedView()` with a `TemplateRef`, what precise lifecycle and structural mechanics occur regarding custom structural directives and deferred hydration?
options: It queues the view creation asynchronously until the Angular hydration microtask queue is fully flushed, preventing immediate DOM presence.
It compiles the template string dynamically at runtime into an intermediate Abstract Syntax Tree before appending it to the DOM renderer.
It automatically wraps the generated nodes inside an Angular-managed `ng-container` anchor element that remains permanently visible in the DOM.

It instantiates the template nodes, attaches the view to the ViewContainerRef tree, inserts the DOM elements immediately into the parent element's location, and runs change detection during the next application tick unless detached.
questions.correctAnswer: It instantiates the template nodes, attaches the view to the ViewContainerRef tree, inserts the DOM elements immediately into the parent element's location, and runs change detection during the next application tick unless detached.
questions.explanation: Calling createEmbeddedView immediately instantiates the template content into DOM nodes, inserts them into the DOM at the ViewContainerRef's relative position, and adds the newly created EmbeddedViewRef to the container's internal view list, participating in subsequent change detection cycles.
questions.hint: Consider whether ViewContainerRef operations are synchronous or queued during view instantiation.
questions.relatedConcept: ViewContainerRef and EmbeddedView instantiation lifecycle
questions.interviewTip: Be prepared to explain how dynamic structural directives manipulate host elements and view trees without triggering full component re-bootstrap.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q16] What is the internal execution consequence when an Angular InjectionToken is provided with `providedIn: 'root'` while simultaneously being included in a lazy-loaded feature module's `providers` array?
options: The lazy-loaded module creates a new, isolated injector scope that shadows the root instance, resulting in a distinct service instance being injected into components within that lazy module.
Angular throws a runtime CyclicDependencyError during module initialization because a root-scoped provider cannot be redeclared.
The root-scoped singleton instance is automatically overridden across the entire application, including eagerly loaded components.
Angular merges the provider definitions at compile time, eliminating the duplicate declaration and preserving a single global singleton.
questions.correctAnswer: The lazy-loaded module creates a new, isolated injector scope that shadows the root instance, resulting in a distinct service instance being injected into components within that lazy module.
questions.explanation: Lazy-loaded modules in Angular have their own child injector hierarchy. Providing a token that is already registered with 'root' inside a lazy module's providers array causes the lazy injector to create a new instance local to that lazy module and its children, shadowing the root singleton.
questions.hint: Think about Angular's hierarchical injector tree and how lazy-loaded modules construct child injectors.
questions.relatedConcept: Hierarchical Injectors and module provider shadowing
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of Angular's module and element injector trees, particularly potential memory or state bugs caused by accidental shadowing.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q17] When implementing custom structural directives in Angular using `TemplateRef` and `ViewContainerRef`, what is the primary execution consequence of using `EmbeddedViewRef.destroy()` versus relying solely on `ViewContainerRef.clear()` or structural micro-syntax bindings?
options: Calling `EmbeddedViewRef.destroy()` automatically unlinks the view from the parent `ViewContainerRef` internal indices, mirroring the behavior of `ViewContainerRef.clear()` while freeing memory immediately.

Calling `EmbeddedViewRef.destroy()` permanently detaches and destroys the view, running DOM teardown and triggering associated change detection cleanup, but it leaves the internal tracking pointer inside `ViewContainerRef` stale until explicitly removed from its container index.
Calling `EmbeddedViewRef.destroy()` throws a runtime compilation error because embedded views can only be destroyed via `ViewContainerRef` methods.
Calling `EmbeddedViewRef.destroy()` detaches the view from the DOM renderer but retains all associated DOM element references in memory indefinitely to optimize subsequent view recreation.
questions.correctAnswer: Calling `EmbeddedViewRef.destroy()` permanently detaches and destroys the view, running DOM teardown and triggering associated change detection cleanup, but it leaves the internal tracking pointer inside `ViewContainerRef` stale until explicitly removed from its container index.
questions.explanation: An `EmbeddedViewRef` maintains its own lifecycle separate from the container's array index management. Calling `destroy()` on the view ref cleans up the view's bindings, injectors, and DOM nodes, but the parent `ViewContainerRef` may still hold a reference to the destroyed view instance in its internal views collection until explicitly detached or cleared via container methods.
questions.hint: Consider the relationship between individual view references and the container that instantiated them.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular structural directives and view lifecycle management via ViewContainerRef and EmbeddedViewRef
questions.interviewTip: Intervers use this to test deep knowledge of Angular's renderer internals and memory leak vectors in custom structural directives.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q18] How does Angular's dependency injection system resolve providers when an InjectionToken is provided across multiple hierarchical injector boundaries, specifically when using 'environmentProviders' introduced in Angular 14+ via `makeEnvironmentProviders` versus traditional NgModule providers?
options: Providers created via `makeEnvironmentProviders` (environmentProviders) are strictly restricted to application-root or lazy-loaded route injectors and cannot be overridden by component-level or NgModule-level injectors.
Environment providers merge with NgModule providers automatically, giving NgModule providers higher precedence during resolution to ensure backward compatibility.

Environment providers (`makeEnvironmentProviders`) restrict provider scope so they cannot be accidentally imported into component `providers` arrays, preventing accidental hierarchical shadowing and mixing of element-level and platform-level dependencies.
Environment providers bypass the hierarchical tree entirely and register directly into the global static root injector regardless of lazy loading boundaries.
questions.correctAnswer: Environment providers (`makeEnvironmentProviders`) restrict provider scope so they cannot be accidentally imported into component `providers` arrays, preventing accidental hierarchical shadowing and mixing of element-level and platform-level dependencies.
questions.explanation: Angular introduced `makeEnvironmentProviders` to separate environment-scoped providers (like HTTP interceptors, router configs) from element-scoped providers (components and directives). A key architectural safety feature is that TypeScript types prevent environment-only providers from being mistakenly added to a component's `providers` array.
questions.hint: Think about why Angular 14 split providers into environmentProviders and regular providers regarding component injectors.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Standalone Components, environmentProviders, and hierarchical dependency injection separation
questions.interviewTip: Expect this question when senior roles require mastery over Angular's migration to standalone APIs and modern DI encapsulation.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q19] When debugging an Angular application using TestBed in a unit test, what is the precise side effect of calling 'TestBed.compileComponents()' asynchronously before creating a component instance?
options: It compiles the entire TypeScript project down to ES2015 bytecode inside the testing browser context.
It forces Angular's zone to flush all pending microtasks and macrotasks prior to instantiating the DOM fixture.
It builds the production-optimized ahead-of-time (AOT) dependency injection dependency graph for the test suite.
It fetches external HTML and CSS template files via XHR/fetch when component decorators use relative templateUrl or styleUrls paths.
questions.correctAnswer: It fetches external HTML and CSS template files via XHR/fetch when component decorators use relative templateUrl or styleUrls paths.
questions.explanation: In Angular's testing environment, components often use relative paths for external templates and stylesheets. Because these must be loaded asynchronously over the network or via file systems, 'compileComponents()' resolves this asynchronous fetching phase before TestBed.createComponent() is called synchronously.
questions.hint: Think about what JIT (Just-in-Time) compilation needs to resolve when templates are stored in separate files referenced relatively.
questions.relatedConcept: TestBed compileComponents asynchronous fixture initialization
questions.interviewTip: Intervers ask this to ensure candidates understand why async/await or beforeEach with async is required in Angular TestBed setups when using external templates.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q20] How does Angular's dependency injection hierarchy behave when a service is provided via '@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })' versus being declared in a lazy-loaded feature module's 'providers' array?
options: 'providedIn: 'root'' creates a single application-wide singleton instance, whereas a lazy-loaded module's 'providers' array creates a scoped injector instance unique to that lazy-loaded chunk.
Both approaches result in an identical application-wide singleton instance shared across all eager and lazy chunks.
A lazy-loaded module's 'providers' array takes precedence, shadowing the 'root' provider and instantiating a new copy even for eager modules.
'providedIn: 'root'' creates a new singleton per lazy-loaded boundary, while feature module providers are strictly scoped to the root injector.
questions.correctAnswer: 'providedIn: 'root'' creates a single application-wide singleton instance, whereas a lazy-loaded module's 'providers' array creates a scoped injector instance unique to that lazy-loaded chunk.
questions.explanation: Services with 'providedIn: 'root'' are registered in the root injector, making them singletons across the entire app. Conversely, when a service is listed in a lazy-loaded module's 'providers' array, Angular creates a child injector specifically for that lazy-loaded module, resulting in a separate instance of that service isolated to that lazy subtree.
questions.hint: Consider how lazy loading introduces isolated injector child boundaries in Angular's hierarchical dependency injection system.
questions.relatedConcept: Hierarchical Dependency Injection and Lazy Loaded Module Injector Scoping
questions.interviewTip: Crucial for diagnosing state-leakage bugs where developers accidentally instantiate multiple service copies instead of maintaining a true singleton.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q21] When leveraging Angular's `bypassSecurityTrustHtml` sanitizer method to render dynamic HTML content, which of the following security implications applies?
options: It permanently disables the sanitizer globally across the entire Angular application instance for all subsequent template bindings.
It disables Angular's built-in contextual sanitization for that specific binding, allowing arbitrary script execution (XSS) if the input contains malicious payloads.
It sanitizes the string by stripping dangerous script tags while securely preserving safe formatting elements.
It throws a runtime exception if the provided string contains any unescaped characters or HTML tags.
questions.correctAnswer: It disables Angular's built-in contextual sanitization for that specific binding, allowing arbitrary script execution (XSS) if the input contains malicious payloads.
questions.explanation: The DomSanitizer methods like bypassSecurityTrustHtml tell Angular's template engine to trust a value as safe for a specific context (HTML, Style, Script, URL, etc.), effectively disabling the built-in automatic sanitization for that binding. If user-supplied input is passed directly without prior rigorous sanitization, this leads to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).
questions.hint: Think about what 'bypass' means regarding Angular's built-in XSS protections.
questions.relatedConcept: DomSanitizer bypass security trust misuse and XSS vulnerabilities
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers often ask this to verify if candidates understand the security risks associated with disabling Angular's default sanitization framework.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q22] What is the primary security risk of misusing Angular's `DOCUMENT` injection token to manipulate the DOM directly within component code rather than using Renderer2 or template bindings?
options: It causes a memory leak because injected document tokens are never garbage collected by the Angular platform injector.
It violates Angular's strict encapsulation rules, causing the Dependency Injection container to throw a NullInjectorError at runtime.

Bypassing Angular's abstraction layers removes the automated sanitization protections applied to standard template bindings, potentially creating DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vectors if working with raw user input.
It forces the component to run outside the Angular Zone, completely breaking change detection synchronization.
questions.correctAnswer: Bypassing Angular's abstraction layers removes the automated sanitization protections applied to standard template bindings, potentially creating DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vectors if working with raw user input.
questions.explanation: Directly manipulating the DOM via native APIs like `innerHTML` using the injected `DOCUMENT` token bypasses Angular's built-in template binding security and sanitization pipeline, leading to security vulnerabilities if unvalidated user input is injected directly.
questions.hint: Consider how native DOM manipulation compares to Angular's template binding pipeline regarding security checks.
questions.relatedConcept: DOCUMENT token misuse and bypass of template sanitization
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test deep knowledge of Angular's security architecture beyond basic component creation.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q23] When utilizing Angular's `NgZone.runOutsideAngular` to execute a heavy, third-party non-Angular asynchronous operation, what is the primary architectural implication regarding change detection and UI responsiveness?
options: The code inside will execute in a separate Web Worker thread automatically to prevent blocking the main JS thread.
Angular will automatically throw an execution error because asynchronous timers are strictly forbidden outside `NgZone`.
Change detection will run twice as fast because the framework prioritizes tasks executed in the outer zone.
Callbacks executed inside the callback block will bypass the Angular zone entirely, preventing microtasks and macrotasks from triggering automatic View/Component dirty-checking cycles.
questions.correctAnswer: Callbacks executed inside the callback block will bypass the Angular zone entirely, preventing microtasks and macrotasks from triggering automatic View/Component dirty-checking cycles.
questions.explanation: Executing code via `runOutsideAngular` detaches the execution context from Angular's custom Zone (`NgZone`). As a result, any asynchronous events (like `setInterval` or DOM events) triggered within that block will not automatically invoke `ApplicationRef.tick()`, saving significant CPU cycles from redundant change detection runs. To update the view, developers must explicitly call `ChangeDetectorRef.detectChanges()` or re-enter the zone.
questions.hint: Think about how Angular knows when to trigger change detection and what happens when an event escapes its wrapped zone.
questions.relatedConcept: NgZone and Performance Optimization
questions.interviewTip: Senior interviewers look for deep understanding of Angular's change detection triggers and how to optimize high-frequency event streams (like mousemove or scroll) using NgZone.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q24] What is the primary architectural difference between an Angular Route Resolver and utilizing `async` pipe inside a component template for data fetching during navigation?
options: Route Resolvers block navigation completion until the observable emits and completes, whereas `async` pipe renders the component immediately and resolves data asynchronously within the template lifecycle.
Route Resolvers automatically cache HTTP requests globally, while `async` pipe forces a fresh server fetch on every template render.
Route Resolvers are exclusively designed for standalone components, whereas `async` pipe only works in NgModule-based applications.
Using an `async` pipe prevents the router from throwing navigation cancellation errors if an HTTP request fails.
questions.correctAnswer: Route Resolvers block navigation completion until the observable emits and completes, whereas `async` pipe renders the component immediately and resolves data asynchronously within the template lifecycle.
questions.explanation: A Route Resolver runs prior to route activation, delaying the navigation transition until the resolved data is fully available. Conversely, using an `async` pipe lets the component render immediately in a loading state, fetching and rendering the data asynchronously as the observable emits.
questions.hint: Consider the user experience and navigation lifecycle when a slow network request is tied to a route change versus an in-component subscription.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Routers, Resolvers, and Reactive Data Fetching
questions.interviewTip: Interfering with navigation via resolvers can cause perceived performance bottlenecks if not handled properly. Discussing when to use resolvers versus component-level fetching is a hallmark of a senior frontend engineer.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q25] In Angular, when using the `inject()` function outside of an injection context (such as inside a standard asynchronous callback or a custom class method invoked after component initialization), what behavior occurs?
options: It successfully resolves and returns the dependency by capturing the lexical scope of the component instance at compile time.
It throws a RuntimeError because the reactive injection context has been lost outside the synchronous execution of an injection factory or constructor/field initializer.
It returns undefined and logs a warning to the console, allowing graceful degradation of the service lookup.
It falls back to the root injector context automatically, ignoring component-level providers.
questions.correctAnswer: It throws a RuntimeError because the reactive injection context has been lost outside the synchronous execution of an injection factory or constructor/field initializer.
questions.explanation: The `inject()` function relies on a globally maintained tracking mechanism during the execution phase of injection contexts (such as constructor, field initializers, and factory functions). Once control flow leaves the synchronous execution stack (like inside a `setTimeout` callback or an async/await boundary), the active injector context is cleared, causing `inject()` to throw an error.
questions.hint: Think about when the injection context is active during a component's lifecycle and event loop turns.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Dependency Injection Context and inject() mechanics
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify whether the candidate understands the underlying mechanics of modern Angular's `inject()` function versus traditional constructor injection.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q26] What is the primary architectural reason that Angular signals are designed with synchronous pull-based evaluation instead of automatic push-based reactive streams (like RxJS BehaviorSubjects)?
options: To enforce that all state changes must happen exclusively inside Angular Zone.js interception blocks to trigger change detection.
To bypass TypeScript's type checking system for deeply nested reactive data structures.
To guarantee glitch-free execution where derived computations (computed) are evaluated lazily only when read, eliminating redundant intermediate recalculations in diamond dependency graphs.
To allow native browser garbage collection to immediately reclaim memoized values on every read operation.
questions.correctAnswer: To guarantee glitch-free execution where derived computations (computed) are evaluated lazily only when read, eliminating redundant intermediate recalculations in diamond dependency graphs.
questions.explanation: Signals use a pull-based, lazy evaluation model combined with a push notification of dirty state. When a dependency changes, dependents are only marked as dirty. They are not recalculated until explicitly read (pulled). This prevents the 'glitch' problem common in naive push architectures where intermediate values in a diamond dependency graph might be evaluated multiple times.
questions.hint: Consider how computed values decide when to recalculate relative to when they are accessed.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Signals pull-based reactivity and glitch-free evaluation
questions.interviewTip: Crucial question for senior roles to distinguish between RxJS push-based streams and fine-grained signal reactivity.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q27] When using Angular's 'APP_INITIALIZER' injection token to run asynchronous startup tasks before the application completely bootstraps, what happens if one of the provider factories returns an observable that completes without emitting any value?
options: The application bootstrap fails because APP_INITIALIZER expects at least one emitted value from the observable.
Angular ignores the observable entirely and throws a runtime NullInjectorError.
The application enters an infinite bootstrap loading state waiting for a emission.
Angular waits for the observable to complete and successfully proceeds with application bootstrapping.
questions.correctAnswer: Angular waits for the observable to complete and successfully proceeds with application bootstrapping.
questions.explanation: Angular's APP_INITIALIZER relies on 'toPromise()' or firstValueFrom-like resolution under the hood which resolves upon completion of the returned Promise/Observable. Emitting a value is not strictly required as long as the observable successfully completes.
questions.hint: Consider whether completion alone is sufficient or if an emission is mandatory for stream resolution.
questions.relatedConcept: APP_INITIALIZER stream completion semantics
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of RxJS stream lifecycles in conjunction with Angular's core platform initialization tokens.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q28] In an Angular application utilizing Zone.js, what is the precise side-effect of executing an asynchronous task inside a function wrapped with 'NgZone.runOutsideAngular' when that task eventually mutates a component property bound in the template?
options: The component property updates in memory, but the view does not reflect the change immediately because no change detection cycle is scheduled by Zone.js.
The component property updates immediately, and Angular automatically triggers a change detection cycle because Zone.js intercepts all timers.
Angular throws a NgZoneOptimizedExecutionError preventing mutations outside the zone.
The application crashes due to a cross-zone thread synchronization violation.
questions.correctAnswer: The component property updates in memory, but the view does not reflect the change immediately because no change detection cycle is scheduled by Zone.js.
questions.explanation: When code runs outside the Angular zone, asynchronous callbacks like setTimeout do not trigger Angular's automatic change detection mechanism. The model updates, but the DOM view remains stale until another event forces change detection.
questions.hint: Think about what Zone.js listens to in order to trigger automatic change detection cycles.
questions.relatedConcept: NgZone runOutsideAngular change detection implication
questions.interviewTip: Crucial for performance tuning discussions where developers optimize high-frequency events (like mousemoves) by bypassing change detection.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q29] When leveraging Angular's `NgZone.runOutsideAngular` to execute high-frequency DOM event handlers or third-party animations, what is the precise performance implication on change detection cycles?
options: It completely disables Zone.js globally across the entire application instance for the lifetime of the component.
It prevents Zone.js from intercepting the macro/microtasks inside the callback, halting automatic dirty-checking propagation for that event stream until manually re-entered or triggered.
It converts synchronous event emissions into asynchronous Promises, delaying execution until the next microtask queue flush.
It forces the component to permanently switch to OnPush change detection strategy, ignoring all subsequent @Input changes.
questions.correctAnswer: It prevents Zone.js from intercepting the macro/microtasks inside the callback, halting automatic dirty-checking propagation for that event stream until manually re-entered or triggered.
questions.explanation: Executing code via `runOutsideAngular` detaches the specified execution context from Zone.js interception. Consequently, asynchronous operations or events triggered within this block do not automatically notify Angular to run a global change detection pass, drastically reducing CPU overhead during high-frequency events.
questions.hint: Consider how Zone.js hooks into asynchronous operations and how Angular's tick() gets triggered.
questions.relatedConcept: NgZone optimization and change detection mitigation
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to test whether candidates understand how Angular bridges underlying browser events to framework-level change detection via Zone.js.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q30] In an Angular application utilizing `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`, under which specific condition will a component NOT re-render even when a local service injected into it updates its internal RxJS BehaviorSubject state?
options: It will always re-render automatically because BehaviorSubject triggers an immediate change detection cycle upon emission.
It will fail to re-render if the service method is invoked from outside the Angular zone.
If the template does NOT use the async pipe, or if the service instance is scoped locally via component providers rather than 'root'.
It will not re-render if the component has child components using Default change detection.
questions.correctAnswer: If the template does NOT use the async pipe, or if the service instance is scoped locally via component providers rather than 'root'.
questions.explanation: With `OnPush`, Angular only checks a component if an `@Input` reference changes, an event originates from the component/children, or an async pipe receives a new emission. If the service is injected and state is mutated/emitted without an async pipe binding in the template or an explicit `markForCheck()` call, OnPush prevents the view from updating.
questions.hint: Remember that OnPush components are immune to service state mutations unless explicitly flagged or bound via specific pipes.
questions.relatedConcept: OnPush change detection and reactive state binding mechanisms
questions.interviewTip: This tests the boundary between RxJS observables and Angular's rendering lifecycle optimization under OnPush.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'OnPush' change detection strategy, which of the following scenarios will successfully trigger a component update even if the inputs remain referentially identical?
options: A standard browser event listener registered via 'addEventListener' inside the component fires.
An Observable input connected via the 'async' pipe emits a new value.
A 'setTimeout' callback executes inside the component without manual ChangeDetectorRef interaction.
A property marked with @Input() is modified directly via a class method after the view has initialized.
questions.correctAnswer: An Observable input connected via the 'async' pipe emits a new value.
questions.explanation: The 'async' pipe automatically calls 'markForCheck()' on the ChangeDetectorRef whenever the associated Observable emits, which flags the component (and its ancestors) as dirty for the next check. Standard browser event listeners or raw setTimeout callbacks are outside of Angular's zone-aware monkey-patching in specific environments or don't automatically trigger CD for OnPush components without an explicit call to 'markForCheck()' or 'detectChanges()'.
questions.hint: Consider how the async pipe interacts with the ChangeDetectorRef internally.
questions.relatedConcept: OnPush Change Detection Strategy
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate to explain why 'OnPush' is often considered a performance optimization but can lead to 'UI not updating' bugs.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush' strategy, which of the following scenarios will trigger a change detection cycle for a component instance?
options: A service injected into the component emits a new value via a BehaviorSubject that is not bound to an @Input() property.
An event listener attached to a child element inside the component's template fires, causing the component's reference-type @Input() property to be marked for check.
An asynchronous timer (setTimeout) completes within the component class, even if no @Input() properties have changed.
The component's reference-type @Input() property is updated using a mutation operation (e.g., array.push()).
questions.correctAnswer: An event listener attached to a child element inside the component's template fires, causing the component's reference-type @Input() property to be marked for check.
questions.explanation: With OnPush, change detection is only triggered if an @Input() reference changes, an event originates from the component or its children, or an Observable bound via the 'async' pipe emits. Mutations do not trigger detection because the reference remains the same. A Service emission or internal timer does not automatically trigger detection unless an event is dispatched or the component is manually marked for check.
questions.hint: Consider the mechanisms that mark a component as dirty when using OnPush.
questions.relatedConcept: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush lifecycle and zone interaction
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands the difference between Zone.js-triggered detection and the specific constraints of OnPush components.

title: Angular - Test 2: Technical Assessment
description: Test 2 for Angular. Every question is unique against the whole question database — no repeats, no renumbered or reworded variants of an existing question.

questions.question: What is the primary runtime performance advantage of Angular's new signal-based reactivity model over traditional Zone.js-based change detection?
options: It entirely prevents JavaScript garbage collection by pre-allocating memory blocks for all component state variables during bootstrap.
It eliminates the need to run change detection over the entire component tree by targeting updates directly to the affected DOM nodes or dependent computations.
It completely bypasses the browser's main thread by executing all reactive graph evaluations inside Web Workers.
It automatically converts all RxJS Observables into native Promise chains to reduce microtask queue contention.
questions.correctAnswer: It eliminates the need to run change detection over the entire component tree by targeting updates directly to the affected DOM nodes or dependent computations.
questions.explanation: Signals provide fine-grained reactivity, allowing Angular to know precisely which components or template bindings depend on a specific value. Consequently, when a signal changes, Angular only re-evaluates the exact dependent nodes rather than traversing and checking the entire component subtree as Zone.js does.
questions.hint: Think about what Zone.js forces Angular to do globally versus what fine-grained reactive primitives know about their consumers.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular signal fine-grained reactivity performance trade-offs
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if the candidate understands the fundamental shift in Angular's rendering architecture from coarse-grained component tree traversal to fine-grained dependency graphs.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'ViewChild' decorator to query a component or directive, what is the impact of setting the 'static' option to 'true' vs 'false'?
options: If set to 'true', the element is updated automatically during every change detection cycle; if 'false', it is updated only once.
If set to 'true', the element is available in 'ngOnInit'; if 'false', it is only available in 'ngAfterViewInit'.
If set to 'true', the query ignores any elements inside *ngIf or *ngFor blocks; if 'false', it includes them.
If set to 'true', the query is performed asynchronously; if 'false', it is performed synchronously at compile time.
questions.correctAnswer: If set to 'true', the element is available in 'ngOnInit'; if 'false', it is only available in 'ngAfterViewInit'.
questions.explanation: Setting 'static: true' instructs Angular to resolve the query before change detection runs, making it available in 'ngOnInit'. Setting it to 'false' (the default for many cases) waits until change detection completes, requiring 'ngAfterViewInit' to access the element safely.
questions.hint: Think about the lifecycle hooks and when the DOM is guaranteed to be rendered.
questions.relatedConcept: ViewChild static resolution
questions.codeSnippet: @ViewChild('target', { static: false }) element!: ElementRef;
questions.interviewTip: Candidates often struggle with 'ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError' which is frequently caused by incorrect static resolution settings.

questions.question: When defining an Angular Provider using the 'useFactory' property, what is the primary purpose of the 'deps' (dependencies) array?
options: To define the order in which services are instantiated across the entire application module tree.
To register the service in the DI container so it can be tree-shaken by the Angular compiler.
To explicitly list the injection tokens required by the factory function for dependency injection.
To perform a lazy-loading check on the provided dependencies before the factory is executed.
questions.correctAnswer: To explicitly list the injection tokens required by the factory function for dependency injection.
questions.explanation: The 'deps' array tells the Dependency Injection system which services or tokens to inject into the factory function as arguments. Without this, the DI container would not know which instances to pass to the factory function.
questions.hint: The factory function needs to receive its arguments from somewhere.
questions.relatedConcept: Dependency Injection Factory Providers
questions.codeSnippet: { provide: ServiceA, useFactory: (s: ServiceB) => new ServiceA(s), deps: [ServiceB] }
questions.interviewTip: Understanding factory providers is crucial for advanced DI scenarios, like conditional service instantiation or configuring third-party libraries.

questions.question: When utilizing the `ViewContainerRef.createEmbeddedView()` method to instantiate a template, what happens to the template's internal state if the host component is destroyed before the view is detached?
options: The view remains in the DOM until manually removed by the parent component.
The view triggers a 'detached' lifecycle hook on the component.
The view remains as a memory leak until the browser process terminates.
The view is automatically destroyed and its associated nodes are removed from the DOM.
questions.correctAnswer: The view is automatically destroyed and its associated nodes are removed from the DOM.
questions.explanation: Angular's ViewContainerRef manages the lifecycle of views it creates. When the host component is destroyed, Angular recursively destroys all embedded views attached to its ViewContainerRef, ensuring that DOM nodes are cleaned up and memory is released.
questions.hint: Consider the relationship between a component's lifecycle and its child view containers.
questions.relatedConcept: Component and View lifecycle management
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how Angular handles child view clean-up is crucial for avoiding memory leaks in dynamic UI components.

questions.question: In a scenario where a child component uses the 'OnPush' change detection strategy, what is the specific effect on change detection if a parent component uses a 'ChangeDetectorRef.detectChanges()' call within an event listener?
options: It triggers change detection for the parent and its children, even if the child's input properties remain unchanged.
It triggers change detection only for the parent component, skipping OnPush children entirely.
It force-updates the child component regardless of its own OnPush configuration, but only if they share the same change detection tree.
It throws a runtime error because ChangeDetectorRef.detectChanges() is forbidden on OnPush components.
questions.correctAnswer: It triggers change detection for the parent and its children, even if the child's input properties remain unchanged.
questions.explanation: Calling detectChanges() explicitly on a component tells Angular to run change detection starting from that component downwards. This bypasses the typical OnPush 'check-only-on-input-change' restriction, forcing all child components in that subtree to undergo change detection.
questions.hint: Think about the scope of the ChangeDetectorRef methods.
questions.relatedConcept: Change detection propagation and force-checking
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate about the performance implications of manual change detection versus using AsyncPipe.

questions.question: In Angular, when utilizing the 'defer' block with the 'on viewport' trigger, which intersection observer property determines whether the deferred content is swapped back to the placeholder if the element leaves the screen?
options: The browser's native intersection ratio threshold setting specified in the defer config.
The viewport trigger behavior is strictly 'lazy-load once'; the content remains rendered once instantiated.
It is determined by the 'on idle' configuration if paired with the viewport trigger.
The internal 'isIntersecting' flag requires manual cleanup via a custom directive to revert to placeholder.
questions.correctAnswer: The viewport trigger behavior is strictly 'lazy-load once'; the content remains rendered once instantiated.
questions.explanation: The Angular @defer block with the 'on viewport' trigger is designed for lazy loading. Once the deferred block is loaded and rendered, the placeholder is removed permanently. It does not natively toggle back to the placeholder when the element leaves the viewport.
questions.hint: Think about the lifecycle of lazy-loaded components in the defer block.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Deferrable Views
questions.codeSnippet: @defer (on viewport) { <large-component /> } @placeholder { <loader /> }
questions.interviewTip: Assess if the candidate understands that deferrable views are for optimization (loading performance), not for dynamic visibility toggling.

questions.question: When using 'ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush', which specific action results in the component NOT being marked for check by the Angular change detector?
options: Updating the reference of a deep property inside an object passed as an Input.
Triggering a DOM event bound via (@event) inside the component template.
Executing an asynchronous 'setTimeout' that updates a class member property.
Invoking 'ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck()' from within a service subscription.
questions.correctAnswer: Executing an asynchronous 'setTimeout' that updates a class member property.
questions.explanation: OnPush only marks a component for check on: Input reference changes, AsyncPipe emissions, or explicit detector triggers. A standard 'setTimeout' callback does not notify the detector unless manually triggered, unlike DOM events which are intercepted by Zone.js.
questions.hint: Remember that Zone.js wraps browser events, but doesn't track arbitrary timer callbacks automatically for OnPush components.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Change Detection Strategy
questions.codeSnippet: @Component({ changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush }) class DataComponent { @Input() data: any; }
questions.interviewTip: Distinguish between Zone.js event patching and the internal behavior of the OnPush change detection mechanism.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush' strategy, which specific lifecycle hook or event triggers a check if the component's input reference has not changed?
options: The component is automatically checked after every microtask completion regardless of event sources.
The component is checked every time the parent component's ngDoCheck runs, regardless of input state.
The component is checked only when the 'ngAfterContentChecked' hook is invoked by the renderer.
The component is only checked when an Input reference changes, an event originated from the component/children occurs, or markForCheck() is called.
questions.correctAnswer: The component is only checked when an Input reference changes, an event originated from the component/children occurs, or markForCheck() is called.
questions.explanation: OnPush strategy disables automatic check-on-every-event, restricting the change detection cycle to: Input reference changes, event listeners attached to the template, or manual signals like markForCheck().
questions.hint: Think about the mechanism that forces a check in a strategy designed for performance optimization.
questions.relatedConcept: OnPush Change Detection triggers
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands performance optimization boundaries in Angular.

questions.question: In the context of Angular Dependency Injection, what is the primary behavior difference between 'viewProviders' and 'providers' within a component's decorator?
options: Services defined in 'viewProviders' are inaccessible to projected content (ng-content), whereas 'providers' are accessible to all children.
Services in 'viewProviders' are singleton-scoped, while 'providers' are prototype-scoped per component instance.
There is no difference in runtime behavior; 'viewProviders' is merely a deprecated alias for 'providers'.
Services in 'viewProviders' are automatically destroyed when the view is detached, while 'providers' persist until the component is destroyed.
questions.correctAnswer: Services defined in 'viewProviders' are inaccessible to projected content (ng-content), whereas 'providers' are accessible to all children.
questions.explanation: viewProviders scope services specifically to the component's internal view tree, excluding components injected via ng-content, which is a common pattern for encapsulation.
questions.hint: Consider how Dependency Injection interacts with Content Projection.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Dependency Injection Scoping
questions.interviewTip: Ask this to see if the candidate knows how to handle injection scope for reusable components with templates.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the `DestroyRef` injection token in a standalone component or service, what is the primary advantage of calling `destroyRef.onDestroy()` versus manually implementing the `OnDestroy` lifecycle hook?
options: It forces an immediate garbage collection of all injected dependencies associated with the instance.
It decouples cleanup logic from the component class, allowing it to be encapsulated within reusable providers or helper functions.
It provides a mechanism to prevent the component from being destroyed until a specific asynchronous task finishes.
It significantly improves the performance of the Change Detection cycle by bypassing the standard lifecycle queue.
questions.correctAnswer: It decouples cleanup logic from the component class, allowing it to be encapsulated within reusable providers or helper functions.
questions.explanation: DestroyRef allows for registering teardown logic outside of the class itself, facilitating better composition and reuse, whereas OnDestroy is strictly bound to the class instance.
questions.hint: Consider modularity and whether the logic needs to live inside the component class definition.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Dependency Injection and DestroyRef lifecycle management
questions.interviewTip: Ask about this to check if the candidate understands modern Angular composition patterns vs legacy class-based hooks.

questions.question: When utilizing `ChangeDetectorRef.detach()` in an Angular component, what is the specific consequence regarding the component's interaction with the global Zone.js monkey-patched events?
options: The component will immediately stop receiving event emissions from internal @Output emitters.
The component remains responsive to all browser events, but will only update the DOM if the parent component is marked as Dirty.
The component is excluded from automatic change detection cycles initiated by Zone.js, meaning it will not re-render unless explicitly triggered.
The component forces an immediate transition to an OnPush detection strategy regardless of the component's declared strategy.
questions.correctAnswer: The component is excluded from automatic change detection cycles initiated by Zone.js, meaning it will not re-render unless explicitly triggered.
questions.explanation: Detaching the change detector removes it from the tree that Angular traverses during change detection, effectively silencing automatic updates until reattached or manually triggered.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the change detection tree when a node is detached.
questions.relatedConcept: Manual Change Detection control
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands the boundaries of Zone.js and manual performance optimizations.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'defer' block with the 'on idle' trigger, what determines the timing of the content rendering?
options: The content renders immediately after the component's ngOnInit cycle completes.
The content renders only when the user scrolls the defer element into the viewport.
The content renders after a hardcoded 500ms delay to ensure main thread stability.
The content renders after the browser's requestIdleCallback is invoked.
questions.correctAnswer: The content renders after the browser's requestIdleCallback is invoked.
questions.explanation: The 'on idle' trigger leverages the browser's native requestIdleCallback API, which schedules the defer block's content to load when the main thread is not heavily utilized, optimizing perceived performance. Option 2 is incorrect because it relates to component lifecycle, not idle-time scheduling.
questions.hint: Think about how modern browsers schedule non-urgent tasks during quiet periods.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Deferrable Views
questions.codeSnippet: @defer (on idle) { <heavy-component /> }
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate how deferrable views impact Core Web Vitals to assess their architectural knowledge.

questions.question: What is the consequence of modifying a Signal's value during the 'effect' execution phase when 'allowSignalWrites' is not explicitly enabled?
options: Angular throws a runtime error preventing circular dependencies and infinite feedback loops.
The effect executes silently but the change is batched until the next microtask.
The signal update triggers a nested change detection cycle that updates the DOM synchronously.
The effect is automatically converted into a computed property to maintain state consistency.
questions.correctAnswer: Angular throws a runtime error preventing circular dependencies and infinite feedback loops.
questions.explanation: Angular's 'effect' function is designed to prevent side effects that create infinite loops. Writing to a signal inside an effect that is subscribed to that same signal without explicit 'allowSignalWrites: true' triggers a runtime error. Option 1 is incorrect because Angular prevents this by design, it does not batch or convert it.
questions.hint: Consider the relationship between change detection cycles and circular reactivity.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Signals and Side Effects
questions.codeSnippet: effect(() => { count.set(count() + 1); });
questions.interviewTip: Use this to see if the candidate understands the difference between reactive triggers and side-effect management in Angular.

questions.question: In an Angular application, when a component implements the 'AfterContentChecked' lifecycle hook, why might you observe unexpected template flickering or 'ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError' when updating a parent-provided property within that hook?
options: The hook is intended to be synchronous, but the DOM rendering engine treats any property assignment inside it as an asynchronous microtask.
The hook runs after the change detection cycle has already verified the view, and modifying state here triggers a new verification cycle that conflicts with the previous one.
The 'AfterContentChecked' hook only fires when the parent component explicitly invokes a manual change detection update via ChangeDetectorRef.
The hook does not have access to the component's internal state unless the component is decorated with the @Injectable decorator.
questions.correctAnswer: The hook runs after the change detection cycle has already verified the view, and modifying state here triggers a new verification cycle that conflicts with the previous one.
questions.explanation: AfterContentChecked runs after the change detection run for the component's content has completed. Changing state here modifies the view model after it has been checked, violating the unidirectional data flow principle and causing the runtime error in development mode.
questions.hint: Consider the order of operations in the Angular change detection cycle and the unidirectional data flow requirement.
questions.relatedConcept: Lifecycle hook execution timing and change detection constraints
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands that lifecycle hooks are not just event triggers, but have specific implications for Angular's internal state reconciliation.

questions.question: When utilizing the 'provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()' configuration in Angular 18+, what is the fundamental impact on how the application handles template updates compared to the traditional Zone.js approach?
options: The entire component tree is automatically checked every 16ms to ensure synchronization without needing Zone.js hooks.
Angular reverts to a polling mechanism that inspects the DOM for changes rather than tracking object state mutations.
Template updates only occur when Signals used in the template are updated or when markForCheck() is manually called.
Change detection becomes strictly reactive, forcing all templates to be wrapped in an 'Observable' wrapper or they will fail to compile.
questions.correctAnswer: Template updates only occur when Signals used in the template are updated or when markForCheck() is manually called.
questions.explanation: Zoneless change detection removes the reliance on monkey-patching asynchronous APIs (Zone.js). Instead, it relies on explicit signals or manual marking of components as dirty, leading to more predictable performance and smaller bundle sizes.
questions.hint: Think about what replaces the 'global' notification system that Zone.js provided.
questions.relatedConcept: Zoneless Angular architecture and Signal-based reactivity
questions.interviewTip: Zoneless is the modern direction of Angular. Expect senior developers to know that it shifts the responsibility of change detection from the framework's global monkey-patching to local signal notification.

questions.question: When utilizing the 'inject()' function in Angular outside of a constructor or field initializer, specifically within a lifecycle hook like 'ngOnInit', what is the expected outcome?
options: The injection succeeds normally, as 'inject()' is designed to be called at any point in the component lifecycle.
The injection succeeds, but the 'DataService' instance is only available until 'ngOnInit' completes.
The 'inject()' call results in a compile-time error, as the function is restricted to constructor usage only.
The injection fails and throws an error because 'inject()' can only be called during the instantiation phase of an injection context.
questions.correctAnswer: The injection fails and throws an error because 'inject()' can only be called during the instantiation phase of an injection context.
questions.explanation: The 'inject()' function relies on the active injection context, which is only available during the component's construction phase. Calling it in 'ngOnInit' or other lifecycle hooks occurs after the injection context has been cleared, resulting in a runtime error.
questions.hint: Consider the lifecycle of the dependency injection context versus the lifecycle of an Angular component.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Injection Context limitations
questions.interviewTip: Understanding DI limitations prevents runtime errors when transitioning from constructor-based DI to functional injection.

questions.question: What is the primary technical consequence of using 'ChangeDetectorRef.detach()' on an Angular component that is part of a parent component utilizing the 'Default' change detection strategy?
options: The component is removed from the change detection tree, meaning its own 'check' and all child checks are skipped until 'detectChanges()' is called manually.
The component remains in the change detection tree but its template is never re-rendered.
The component remains in the tree, but input properties (via @Input) will no longer trigger automatic updates in the component template.
The component is destroyed, and all of its current state and references are wiped from the DOM immediately.
questions.correctAnswer: The component is removed from the change detection tree, meaning its own 'check' and all child checks are skipped until 'detectChanges()' is called manually.
questions.explanation: Detaching a component removes it from the change detection tree. Angular's change detection mechanism will skip that component subtree during subsequent cycles, requiring manual triggering via 'detectChanges()' to update the view.
questions.hint: Think about how detach() affects the propagation of the change detection tree.
questions.relatedConcept: Manual Change Detection control
questions.interviewTip: This is a critical concept for performance optimization in high-frequency update scenarios.

questions.question: In an Angular application using the 'OnPush' change detection strategy, which of the following scenarios will force a component to perform change detection without an explicit call to 'ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck()'?
options: An asynchronous event triggered by a standard DOM listener (e.g., 'window.resize') that is not wrapped in a Zone.js task.
An event originating from a template-bound event listener, such as a '(click)' handler.
An update to an 'Input()' property where the reference remains identical but the internal state of the object changes.
A timer created using the native 'window.setTimeout' function outside of the Angular Zone.
questions.correctAnswer: An event originating from a template-bound event listener, such as a '(click)' handler.
questions.explanation: Angular's Zone.js patches asynchronous browser events. When an event listener is defined in a template (like '(click)'), the event is executed within the Angular Zone, which automatically triggers change detection across the component tree, even for OnPush components. Option 3 is correct because it is the standard way to trigger detection. Options 1 and 4 do not trigger detection unless they are inside the NgZone, and Option 2 is incorrect because OnPush only reacts to reference changes in @Input properties.
questions.hint: Consider which asynchronous triggers are automatically patched by Angular's Zone.js.
questions.relatedConcept: OnPush Change Detection and Zone.js
questions.interviewTip: Understand that OnPush components are not 'isolated'—they are just skipped during default change detection cycles unless specific conditions (input ref change, event listener, or explicit marking) are met.
