It places the variable in the global data segment, so its value persists across multiple calls to the function.
It allocates the variable on the stack, but prevents local scope leakage to nested blocks within the function.
It creates a thread-specific copy of the variable, ensuring data isolation in multi-threaded environments.
questions.correctAnswer: It places the variable in the global data segment, so its value persists across multiple calls to the function.
questions.explanation: The `static` keyword inside a function grants the variable static storage duration. This means it is allocated once in the global/static data segment and retains its value between function calls. It is not re-initialized to 0 on subsequent calls; it is only initialized once at program startup (or the first time execution passes the declaration, for non-constant types). Option A is incorrect because it is not re-initialized. Option C is incorrect because it is not on the stack. Option D is incorrect because C does not have inherent thread-local storage for static variables without specific extensions or `__thread`/`_Thread_local` keywords.
questions.hint: Think about where the variable is allocated in memory and when its lifetime begins and ends relative to the function call.
questions.relatedConcept: Static Local Variables and Storage Duration
questions.interviewTip: Tests understanding of storage duration vs. scope and common pitfalls in stateful functions.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q2] According to the ISO C standard, what is the precise evaluation order and side-effect behavior of the expression `x = i++ + i++;` when `i` is initialized to 0?
options: The expression is guaranteed to evaluate to 1 because postfix increment happens after the full expression statement completes.
The behavior is undefined due to multiple unsequenced modifications of the object `i` between consecutive sequence points / sequence-point violations.
The expression evaluates safely to 1 because left-to-right evaluation order is strictly mandated by modern C standards for all binary operators.
The variable `x` will reliably hold the value 2, incrementing `i` twice during the sub-expression evaluation phase.
questions.correctAnswer: The behavior is undefined due to multiple unsequenced modifications of the object `i` between consecutive sequence points / sequence-point violations.
questions.explanation: According to the C standard (C99/C11/C18), between the previous and next sequence point a scalar object shall have its stored value modified at most once by the evaluation of an expression. In `i++ + i++`, the object `i` is modified twice without an intervening sequence point, resulting in undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Consider the rules regarding modification of scalar objects between sequence points or sequencing rules for the addition operator.
questions.relatedConcept: Undefined Behavior and Evaluation Sequencing
questions.codeSnippet:
int i = 0;
int x = i++ + i++;
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if candidates rely on compiler quirks versus formal language standards regarding sequence points and undefined behavior.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q3] What is the outcome of using the `goto` statement to jump directly into the scope of a variable-length array (VLA) declaration in C99/C11?
options: It executes successfully, allocating the VLA on the stack at the `goto` target label position with automatic zero-initialization.
It causes a segmentation fault at runtime because the stack pointer is not adjusted for the VLA block.
It results in a compile-time error or undefined behavior because jumping into the scope of a variable-length array that bypasses its initialization is explicitly prohibited by the C standard.
It is fully compliant with the ISO C standard provided the VLA does not exceed available stack limits.
questions.correctAnswer: It results in a compile-time error or undefined behavior because jumping into the scope of a variable-length array that bypasses its initialization is explicitly prohibited by the C standard.
questions.explanation: The C standard specifies that a goto statement cannot jump from a point outside the scope of a variable-length array to a point inside it, because doing so would bypass the evaluation of the expression that determines its size and its runtime allocation.
questions.hint: Think about how runtime stack allocation for variable-length arrays interacts with control flow jumps like `goto`.
questions.relatedConcept: Variable Length Arrays (VLAs) and Scope Control Flow
questions.interviewTip: This question tests advanced knowledge of C99 VLA semantics, stack allocation mechanics, and jump restrictions.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q4] What is the exact behavior and safety implication of passing a format specifier string containing user-controlled input directly to the standard library function `printf()` without an explicit format argument?
options: It results in a compile-time error because `printf` requires at least two arguments.
It causes an immediate segmentation fault due to null-pointer dereferencing in the internal formatting buffer.
It is completely safe as long as `user_input` does not contain any newline characters.
It leads to a Format String vulnerability, enabling arbitrary memory reading via stack specifiers like '%x' or memory writing via '%n'.
questions.correctAnswer: It leads to a Format String vulnerability, enabling arbitrary memory reading via stack specifiers like '%x' or memory writing via '%n'.
questions.explanation: Passing an uncontrolled string directly as the format argument to `printf` allows attackers to exploit format string vulnerabilities, leaking stack or heap contents using format tags like `%s` or `%x`, and even corrupting memory with `%n`.
questions.hint: Consider what happens when format specifiers like '%n' or '%x' are interpreted dynamically by variable-argument functions.
questions.relatedConcept: Format String Vulnerabilities
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of secure coding practices and how variable-length argument lists interact with runtime memory layouts.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q5] What is the strict standard-defined consequence of modifying an object modified between two sequence points or without an intervening sequence point, specifically regarding the behavior of expressions like `i = i++`?
options: The behavior is completely undefined according to the C language standard due to unsequenced side effects on the same scalar object.
The variable `i` is guaranteed to be incremented first, and then assigned the original value.
The variable `i` is guaranteed to be assigned the incremented value first, and then incremented again.
It results in a deterministic compile-time error across all conforming C99 and C11 compilers.
questions.correctAnswer: The behavior is completely undefined according to the C language standard due to unsequenced side effects on the same scalar object.
questions.explanation: Evaluating an expression where a scalar object is modified multiple times without an intervening sequence point (or in C11/C17 terms, conflicting evaluations not sequenced relative to each other) invokes undefined behavior. Compilers are not required to catch this at compile-time.
questions.hint: Think about sequence points and unsequenced side effects on the same variable within a single expression.
questions.relatedConcept: Undefined Behavior in Expressions
questions.codeSnippet:
int i = 1;
int result = i = i++;
questions.interviewTip: This tests whether candidates understand the limits of expression evaluation order and the dangerous pitfalls of standard-defined undefined behavior.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q6] What is the exact theoretical complexity and run-time safety implication of using the standard library function `qsort()` compared to a hand-written inline-expanded sorting routine in C?
options: `qsort()` is guaranteed to be implemented using pure quicksort, leading to O(N^2) worst-case time complexity on sorted inputs without internal mitigation.

`qsort()` relies on function pointers for comparisons, introducing indirect branch overhead and potential cache misses per comparison, but guarantees O(N log N) worst-case time using introsort or heapsort in modern implementations.
`qsort()` performs inline expansion of comparison logic via macros, resulting in zero function-call overhead.
`qsort()` uses a stable merge sort algorithm universally across all standard compliance libraries, requiring O(N) auxiliary heap allocation.
questions.correctAnswer: `qsort()` relies on function pointers for comparisons, introducing indirect branch overhead and potential cache misses per comparison, but guarantees O(N log N) worst-case time using introsort or heapsort in modern implementations.
questions.explanation: Standard library `qsort()` takes a comparator function pointer, which prevents the compiler from inlining the comparison logic, resulting in branch penalties and instruction cache misses. Modern C standard libraries (like GNU libc) implement introsort or fallback strategies to avoid O(N^2) worst-case behavior typical of naive quicksort.
questions.hint: Consider how passing function pointers affects compiler optimizations like inlining.
questions.relatedConcept: Library Function Performance Trade-offs and Indirect Branching in C
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to evaluate whether a candidate understands the hardware-level performance penalty of function pointers versus macro-based sorting routines or inline algorithms.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q7] When designing high-throughput network packet parsers in C, what is the primary architectural trade-off of utilizing bitfields within structs to represent non-byte-aligned protocol headers?
options: Bitfields automatically compile down to single-cycle bitwise shift operations on all CPU architectures without exception.
Bitfields enforce strict byte-alignment matching network wire formats, eliminating all protocol parsing overhead.

Bitfield layout, padding, and endianness behavior are implementation-defined by the C standard, making them non-portable and potentially introducing read-modify-write performance penalties on hardware lacking native bit-extraction instructions.
Bitfields prevent the compiler from utilizing vector registers (SIMD) for any subsequent operations on the surrounding struct.
questions.correctAnswer: Bitfield layout, padding, and endianness behavior are implementation-defined by the C standard, making them non-portable and potentially introducing read-modify-write performance penalties on hardware lacking native bit-extraction instructions.
questions.explanation: The C standard leaves the memory layout, packing order, and boundary crossing of bitfields entirely implementation-defined. Additionally, accessing non-aligned or partial-byte bitfields often forces the CPU to execute costly read-modify-write sequences, degrading parsing throughput compared to explicit bitmasking and shifting.
questions.hint: Think about portability guarantees and how processors handle sub-byte data manipulation.
questions.relatedConcept: Struct Bitfields, Implementation-Defined Behavior, and CPU Read-Modify-Write Penalties
questions.interviewTip: Senior systems engineers look for candidates who recognize that high-performance low-level code often avoids C bitfields in favor of explicit bitwise operations and masks to guarantee portability and predictable assembly output.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q8] What is the standard-defined consequence of casting a function pointer to a data pointer type (such as `void *`) or vice versa in C?
options: It is fully guaranteed to work and round-trip successfully on all conforming C implementations.
The compiler is mandated to insert a runtime conversion thunk to preserve function call ABI semantics.
It causes a compile-time error due to incompatible pointer type qualifiers.
The behavior is undefined by the ISO C standard, although some platforms and POSIX standards allow it.
questions.correctAnswer: The behavior is undefined by the ISO C standard, although some platforms and POSIX standards allow it.
questions.explanation: The ISO C standard explicitly states that conversion between function pointers and data pointers (like void *) is undefined behavior. While POSIX and many modern flat-memory architectures permit it, it violates standard-conforming portability.
questions.hint: Think about whether function pointers and data pointers are guaranteed to share the same representation or address space under ISO C.
questions.relatedConcept: Function Pointer and Data Pointer Conversion
questions.codeSnippet:
void (*func)(void) = some_function;
void *ptr = (void *)func; // What does the C standard say about this?
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this when evaluating a candidate's depth regarding standards compliance vs. platform-specific assumptions in systems programming.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q9] When declaring a flexible array member at the end of a struct, why must the containing struct be allocated using dynamic memory allocation rather than as an automatic (stack) variable?
options: Stack allocation would not allocate trailing space for the array elements, causing subsequent writes to corrupt adjacent stack frames.
The compiler prevents automatic instantiation of structs with flexible array members entirely at compile time.
Stack variables do not support pointer arithmetic required to access elements inside the flexible array.
Flexible array members require special segment registers that only heap-allocated memory can provide.
questions.correctAnswer: Stack allocation would not allocate trailing space for the array elements, causing subsequent writes to corrupt adjacent stack frames.
questions.explanation: A flexible array member takes up zero bytes within the struct layout itself. Allocating a struct on the stack only reserves space for the explicitly named members, so writing to the flexible array will overflow the allocated stack boundaries.
questions.hint: Consider how much storage the compiler reserves for a zero-size or flexible array member when calculating sizeof(struct Packet).
questions.relatedConcept: Flexible Array Members and Stack Allocation
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if developers understand struct layout padding, object sizing, and safety hazards of stack vs heap boundaries.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q10] What is the exact standard behavior regarding file positioning and buffering when switching from reading to writing on an update stream (`r+`, `w+`, or `a+`) without an intervening positioning or file operation like `fseek`, `rewind`, or `fflush`?
options: The write operation automatically truncates the rest of the file contents before writing 'X'.
The write operation is guaranteed to fail or produce undefined behavior unless an intervening file positioning function is called.
The write operation succeeds and overwrites the next byte immediately following the last read byte without any restrictions.
The input buffer is completely discarded, and the file pointer resets to the absolute beginning of the file.
questions.correctAnswer: The write operation is guaranteed to fail or produce undefined behavior unless an intervening file positioning function is called.
questions.explanation: According to the ISO C standard, when switching from reading to writing on an update stream without an intervening call to a file positioning function (such as fseek, fsetpos, or rewind) or an fflush operation, the behavior is undefined or restricted, and standard I/O library implementations often fail or misbehave because the internal stream buffers are not properly synchronized between input and output modes.
questions.hint: Check the C standard rules for mixing read and write operations on update streams.
questions.relatedConcept: Stream I/O buffering and mode-switching restrictions
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test deep familiarity with the ISO C standard's edge cases regarding buffered I/O streams and file positioning requirements.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q11] When utilizing variable-length arrays (VLAs) within nested blocks in C99/C11, how does the lifetime and memory reclamation of the VLA allocation behave when control flow exits the block via a `goto` statement jumping *out* of the block scope?
options: The memory allocated for the VLA is automatically reclaimed immediately when the execution leaves the scope via the goto statement.
The memory allocated for the VLA remains on the stack until the enclosing function returns, because stack pointer adjustments for VLAs cannot be easily unwound by arbitrary jumps.
Jumping past a variable-length array declaration via a goto statement results in a compile-time error.
The memory is retained indefinitely on the heap until explicit manual deallocation via a hidden runtime free is triggered.
questions.correctAnswer: Jumping past a variable-length array declaration via a goto statement results in a compile-time error.
questions.explanation: According to the C standard, a `goto` statement is not permitted to jump into the scope of a variable-length array or past a VLA declaration without entering its scope properly. Doing so results in a constraint violation and is caught as a compile-time error by conforming compilers.
questions.hint: Consider the strict lexical scoping rules regarding jumps and variable-length array declarations.
questions.relatedConcept: Variable-Length Arrays (VLAs) scope and control-flow constraints
questions.interviewTip: Advanced C interviews frequently explore VLAs to evaluate whether candidates understand modern C standard constraints and stack management pitfalls.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q12] What is the exact sequencing constraint mandated by the C standard regarding the evaluation of operands of the logical AND operator (&&) and the comma operator (,) with respect to side effects?
options: Only the comma operator guarantees a sequence point between its operands, whereas && evaluates both operands concurrently without sequencing.
Only && guarantees that the left operand's side effects are fully sequenced before the right operand; the comma operator does not enforce sequencing.
Neither operator creates a sequence point; they only guarantee order of evaluation without completing side effects.
Both && and the comma operator enforce a full sequence point (sequenced-before relationship) between the evaluation of the left operand and the right operand.
questions.correctAnswer: Both && and the comma operator enforce a full sequence point (sequenced-before relationship) between the evaluation of the left operand and the right operand.
questions.explanation: According to the C standard (ISO/IEC 9899), both the logical AND operator (&&) and the comma operator (,) create a sequence point (or in C11/C18 terminology, a 'sequenced-before' relation) between the evaluation of their left and right operands. The left operand is fully evaluated, including all side effects, before the evaluation of the right operand begins.
questions.hint: Think about what guarantees side effects of the left operand are completed before the right operand is even touched.
questions.relatedConcept: Sequence Points and Side Effect Ordering
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test deep understanding of the C memory model and undefined behavior resulting from unsequenced modifications.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q13] In C11 and later, what is the precise behavior of atomic operations with `memory_order_relaxed` regarding synchronization and ordering across multiple threads?
options: Memory order relaxed guarantees atomicity and modification order consistency for each individual variable, but provides no synchronization or inter-thread ordering guarantees between different variables.
If r1 == 1, then r2 is guaranteed to be 1 because stores are globally ordered.
Memory_order_relaxed acts as a full hardware memory fence, ensuring that Thread 2 observes the writes in the exact chronological order they were executed by Thread 1.
The code results in undefined behavior due to data races because no mutex was acquired before accessing the atomic variables.
questions.correctAnswer: Memory order relaxed guarantees atomicity and modification order consistency for each individual variable, but provides no synchronization or inter-thread ordering guarantees between different variables.
questions.explanation: `memory_order_relaxed` guarantees that the atomic operation itself is atomic and maintains a single total modification order for each individual atomic object, but it imposes no synchronization or ordering constraints on other reads or writes. Thus, even if Thread 2 sees `y == 1`, reordering by the compiler or CPU can cause `r2` to read `0`.
questions.hint: Relaxed ordering means atomic access, but zero synchronization between independent variables.
questions.relatedConcept: C11 Atomics and Memory Ordering
questions.interviewTip: Crucial for assessing whether a candidate understands lock-free programming primitives beyond simple mutexes.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q14] What does a sporadic crash with a corrupted `next` chunk pointer during a `free()` call typically signify in a C program using standard glibc malloc?
options: Stack overflow caused by deep recursion overwriting the return address of the active frame
Heap corruption caused by an out-of-bounds write or a double-free error occurring earlier in execution
Memory leak where allocated blocks are lost without being tracked by the runtime allocator
Dereferencing a null pointer during allocation metadata lookup
questions.correctAnswer: Heap corruption caused by an out-of-bounds write or a double-free error occurring earlier in execution
questions.explanation: When glibc malloc detects an invalid chunk header or corrupted doubly-linked list pointers (like `next` or `prev` pointers) during a `free()` call, it throws an abort due to detected heap corruption. This is almost always a symptom of a previous buffer overflow, use-after-free, or double-free.
questions.hint: Think about what meta-information malloc stores adjacent to user data chunks on the heap.
questions.relatedConcept: Heap metadata corruption and memory management debugging
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use debugging symptoms to test whether candidates can trace backward from a runtime crash signature to the underlying memory safety bug.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q15] What is the primary implication when a multithreaded C program running on a weakly ordered architecture (like ARM) experiences intermittent data race corruption despite using non-atomic flags without memory barriers?
options: The `volatile` keyword guarantees atomicity but not instruction ordering on all architectures
The stack frame of Thread 1 was invalidated before Thread 2 finished reading the shared variable
The compiler or CPU reordered the load and store instructions across threads, causing Thread 2 to observe 'flag = 1' before 'shared_data = 42'
A segmentation fault occurred because volatile variables cannot be shared across thread stacks
questions.correctAnswer: The compiler or CPU reordered the load and store instructions across threads, causing Thread 2 to observe 'flag = 1' before 'shared_data = 42'
questions.explanation: Volatile in C prevents the compiler from optimizing away memory reads and writes, but it does NOT guarantee CPU-level memory ordering or atomicity on weakly-ordered architectures like ARM or POWER. Out-of-order execution by the CPU or compiler can reorder memory accesses unless explicit memory barriers or C11 atomic operations with proper memory orderings (e.g., `memory_order_acquire`/`release`) are used.
questions.hint: Distinguish between what `volatile` guarantees regarding compiler optimizations versus what modern CPUs do with instruction pipelining.
questions.relatedConcept: Memory reordering, volatile vs atomics, and concurrency bugs
questions.interviewTip: A classic systems question to see if the candidate understands the hardware limits of the `volatile` keyword in multithreaded contexts.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q16] According to the ISO C standard, what is the strict behavior when a source file passed to a translation unit ends with a backslash character ('\') immediately preceding the end-of-file marker?
options: The backslash and the immediately preceding newline (if any) are spliced, and a compiler diagnostic is required if it leaves a trailing incomplete token at EOF.
The compiler automatically inserts a newline character before EOF to complete the splice, preventing compilation errors.
Undefined behavior occurs as phase 2 line-splicing interacts with the physical end-of-file without a terminating newline.
The backslash is treated as a regular literal character and ignored by the phase 2 line-splicing mechanism because it lacks a following newline.
questions.correctAnswer: The backslash is treated as a regular literal character and ignored by the phase 2 line-splicing mechanism because it lacks a following newline.
questions.explanation: According to ISO C translation phases (Phase 2), physical source lines that end with a backslash are spliced with the following line. If a backslash is the very last character of the file, there is no subsequent newline character to splice with, so the backslash is left as-is without triggering line-splicing behavior (though it may cause a syntax error later if it forms an invalid token, but phase 2 itself treats it literally or ignores splicing since no newline follows).
questions.hint: Think about the exact mechanics of phase 2 line splicing and what character must follow the backslash.
questions.relatedConcept: C Translation Phases and Line Splicing
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test deep knowledge of the C preprocessor and translation phases beyond everyday coding.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q17] What is the exact behavior of `asctime_r` when passed a `struct tm` pointer containing out-of-range fields (e.g., tm_hour = 30, tm_mday = 45), assuming standard POSIX compliance?
options: It formats the raw out-of-range values directly without normalization, potentially resulting in nonsensical strings like 'hour:30'.
It successfully formats the string by normalizing the out-of-range values into standard calendar units before formatting.
It returns NULL and sets `errno` to EINVAL because out-of-range components are strictly rejected by thread-safe time conversion functions.
It invokes undefined behavior because time conversion functions do not perform bounds checking on `struct tm` fields.
questions.correctAnswer: It formats the raw out-of-range values directly without normalization, potentially resulting in nonsensical strings like 'hour:30'.
questions.explanation: Functions like `asctime`, `asctime_r`, `ctime`, and `ctime_r` format the members of `struct tm` directly as integer values without performing normalization (unlike `mktime`, which normalizes out-of-range fields). Thus, `asctime_r` will format the raw values directly into the buffer.
questions.hint: Distinguish between functions that normalize calendar times (like mktime) and those that purely format them.
questions.relatedConcept: Standard Library Time Functions Behavior
questions.interviewTip: This tests whether the candidate knows the subtle contract differences between C library formatting functions versus normalization functions.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q18] According to the ISO C standard, what is the strict behavior regarding pointer type aliasing and the optimization implications of the strict aliasing rule?
options: The compiler must automatically insert a type-pun conversion helper, guaranteeing safe bit-pattern interpretation at runtime.
The compiler can assume that pointers of different types (with specific exceptions like char *) do not point to the same memory location, allowing aggressive optimizations.
Accessing an object through a pointer of an incompatible type always invokes a predictable hardware-defined bitcast operation.
Strict aliasing only applies when the 'volatile' keyword is omitted from both pointer declarations.
questions.correctAnswer: The compiler can assume that pointers of different types (with specific exceptions like char *) do not point to the same memory location, allowing aggressive optimizations.
questions.explanation: The C standard's strict aliasing rule (C99 6.5/7) specifies that an object shall have its stored value accessed only by an lvalue of its own type or compatible types, character types, or aggregate/union types containing them. This allows compilers to assume that pointers to distinct types do not alias, enabling optimizations like keeping values in registers across writes. Violating this rule results in undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Think about how type-punning via incompatible pointer casts impacts compiler optimizations.
questions.relatedConcept: Strict Aliasing Rule and Type Punning
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test deep understanding of the ISO C standard beyond basic syntax, particularly regarding compiler optimizations and undefined behavior.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q19] What is the precise guarantee provided by the C standard regarding the representation of padding bytes within structure objects?
options: Padding bytes are guaranteed to be initialized to zero by default-initialization or compound literal creation.
Padding bytes are completely ignored by the CPU bus architecture and never participate in memory comparisons.
Padding bytes hold unspecified values, meaning `memcmp` between two structs with identical member values can return non-zero if padding bytes differ.
Padding bytes are guaranteed to mirror the bit pattern of the preceding member field.
questions.correctAnswer: Padding bytes hold unspecified values, meaning `memcmp` between two structs with identical member values can return non-zero if padding bytes differ.
questions.explanation: The C standard states that padding bytes in structures have unspecified values unless explicitly initialized (e.g., via `memset` or `calloc`). Consequently, comparing two identically-valued structs using `memcmp` can yield false negatives if their uninitialized padding bytes contain different garbage bit patterns from memory or stack allocation.
questions.hint: Consider what happens to structural padding when automatic variables are declared without explicit zero-initialization.
questions.relatedConcept: Structure Padding and Unspecified Values
questions.interviewTip: This tests whether the candidate understands memory layout nuances and the pitfalls of using raw memory comparison functions like `memcmp` on composite types.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q20] What is the standard-defined behavior regarding data visibility and asynchronous signal handlers when modifying a global variable that is not declared as `volatile` or `sig_atomic_t`?
options: Guaranteed to terminate immediately upon signal arrival because modern hardware invalidates the L1 cache on interrupt vectors.
Valid and standard-compliant in C99 and later, provided the variable is declared at file scope with static linkage.
The program will crash with a SIGSEGV because asynchronous signal handlers cannot mutate non-volatile variables.
Undefined behavior, as the compiler may optimize the loop by caching 'flag' in a CPU register and never re-reading it from memory.
questions.correctAnswer: Undefined behavior, as the compiler may optimize the loop by caching 'flag' in a CPU register and never re-reading it from memory.
questions.explanation: According to the C standard, accessing a non-volatile, non-sig_atomic_t variable inside an asynchronous signal handler while it is being read in the main thread leads to undefined behavior. Compilers are free to optimize the `while (!flag)` loop into an infinite loop by reading `flag` into a register once before the loop begins.
questions.hint: Consider compiler optimizations like register promotion for variables accessed across execution contexts.
questions.relatedConcept: Asynchronous Signal Safety and Volatile Semantics
questions.interviewTip: Interweaves systems programming, compiler optimization theory, and safe concurrent signal handling.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q21] When debugging a C program using Valgrind (Memcheck), what does an 'Invalid read of size 4' error specifically indicate about program execution?
options: The program attempted to read 4 bytes from a memory address that is either unallocated, freed, or outside the boundaries of any valid heap/stack block tracked by Memcheck.
The program accessed a memory address that is validly allocated on the heap, but the 4 bytes contain uninitialized garbage values.
The program attempted to write 4 bytes to a read-only data segment (such as a string literal pool).
The pointer used for the read operation was NULL, causing an immediate hardware trap handled by Valgrind.
questions.correctAnswer: The program attempted to read 4 bytes from a memory address that is either unallocated, freed, or outside the boundaries of any valid heap/stack block tracked by Memcheck.
questions.explanation: 'Invalid read' means the program tried to read from an address it does not own or has not allocated. Reading from allocated but uninitialized memory is flagged as 'Uninitialised byte(s)' rather than an invalid read.
questions.hint: Differentiate between reading uninitialized memory versus reading completely unauthorized or out-of-bounds addresses.
questions.relatedConcept: Memory Error Diagnostics with Valgrind
questions.codeSnippet:
int *arr = malloc(sizeof(int) * 10);
int val = arr[10]; // index 10 is out of bounds
questions.interviewTip: Assess the candidate's practical tool fluency in identifying memory safety violations during post-mortem or runtime diagnosis.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q22] What is the primary security flaw when using the format string vulnerability pattern 'printf(user_input);' where user_input is a buffer controlled entirely by an attacker?
options: It inherently causes a stack buffer overflow by copying an unbounded number of bytes into the internal printf buffer.
It allows an attacker to read arbitrary stack and memory locations using format specifiers like '%p' or '%s', and write to memory using '%n'.
It automatically executes arbitrary shellcode injected into the user_input buffer via instruction pointer hijacking.
It triggers an immediate segmentation fault because user_input lacks a trailing null terminator when read via fgets.
questions.correctAnswer: It allows an attacker to read arbitrary stack and memory locations using format specifiers like '%p' or '%s', and write to memory using '%n'.
questions.explanation: Passing an uncontrolled string directly as the format argument of printf allows attackers to exploit format specifiers. '%p' and '%s' leak values from the stack and memory, while '%n' writes the number of characters written so far into a memory address supplied on the stack, enabling arbitrary memory write primitives.
questions.hint: Think about how printf resolves arguments when format specifiers are provided directly via input rather than as a literal string.
questions.relatedConcept: Format String Vulnerabilities
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of how printf parses stack arguments and how missing format parameters lead to arbitrary memory read/write security holes.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q23] What is the main danger of using the `strncat` function incorrectly by calculating the size parameter as the total size of the destination buffer rather than the remaining space?
options: It results in a compile-time error because sizeof cannot be used on arrays passed to library functions.
It automatically truncates the resulting string to fit within 5 bytes, resulting in data loss without memory corruption.

It can lead to a buffer overflow because the third parameter of strncat specifies the maximum number of characters from the source to append, not the total buffer size, ignoring the bytes already occupied.
It causes an immediate integer underflow in the internal bounds checker of strncat.
questions.correctAnswer: It can lead to a buffer overflow because the third parameter of strncat specifies the maximum number of characters from the source to append, not the total buffer size, ignoring the bytes already occupied.
questions.explanation: The third parameter of `strncat(dest, src, n)` specifies the maximum number of *bytes to append from src*, not the total size of `dest`. Passing `sizeof(dest)` tells the function it can write up to 10 characters from the source, ignoring the 5 bytes already used by "Hello", which overflows the 10-byte buffer.
questions.hint: Check the exact semantics of the size parameter in strncat compared to snprintf or strncpy.
questions.relatedConcept: Off-by-one and Buffer Overflow via String Manipulation APIs
questions.codeSnippet:
char dest[10] = "Hello";
strncat(dest, "World!", sizeof(dest));
questions.interviewTip: This tests practical defensive coding awareness regarding common misuse patterns of safe string handling functions like strncat.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q24] What is the precise C standard behavior regarding memory reuse when a block allocated via `malloc` is subsequently freed and a new `malloc` request of the exact same size is made?
options: The C standard strictly mandates that p2 must equal p1 to minimize external memory fragmentation.
p2 is guaranteed to point to a different memory address because freed chunks are quarantined until program termination.
The behavior is undefined because re-allocating a recently freed size triggers a double-free detection routine.
The standard imposes no requirement that p2 equals p1, though many allocators reuse recently freed blocks for efficiency and locality.
questions.correctAnswer: The standard imposes no requirement that p2 equals p1, though many allocators reuse recently freed blocks for efficiency and locality.
questions.explanation: The C standard abstracts memory management implementation details. It does not dictate heap allocation algorithms (such as first-fit, best-fit, or segregated free lists), meaning `p2` returning the same address as `p1` is a common optimization but not a language-level guarantee.
questions.hint: Think about whether the ISO C standard dictates heap layout policies or leaves them to the runtime implementation.
questions.relatedConcept: Heap allocator implementation semantics and C standard guarantees
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates conflate standard language guarantees with specific runtime/OS allocator behaviors.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q25] In C, what is the precise lifetime and linkage status of a string literal such as `"hello"` when used within a translation unit?
options: It has static storage duration, persists for the entire execution of the program, and has no linkage.
It has static storage duration, persists for the entire execution of the program, and has internal or external linkage depending on declaration scope.
It has automatic storage duration tied to the enclosing block scope unless declared with the `static` keyword.
It has allocated storage duration dynamically managed by the loader, similar to the heap.
questions.correctAnswer: It has static storage duration, persists for the entire execution of the program, and has no linkage.
questions.explanation: String literals in C have static storage duration (they exist for the program's lifetime) and they do not have linkage (they are distinct objects even if their contents are identical). Modifying them invokes undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Consider where string literals reside in memory and whether they can be referenced across different files by name (linkage).
questions.relatedConcept: String literal storage duration and linkage rules
questions.codeSnippet: const char *s = "hello";
questions.interviewTip: Crucial for embedded and low-level systems where memory placement and read-only segments matter.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q26] What is the evaluation order and side-effect behavior of the sequence point rules when modifying the same scalar object multiple times within a single expression in ISO C?
options: The expression is guaranteed to evaluate left-to-right, resulting in j = 2 + 2 = 4.
The behavior is undefined because the scalar object 'i' is modified multiple times between sequence points without an intervening sequence point.
The expression is guaranteed to evaluate right-to-left, resulting in j = 3 + 2 = 5.
The compiler will automatically insert a sequence point between operands, resulting in j = 4.
questions.correctAnswer: The behavior is undefined because the scalar object 'i' is modified multiple times between sequence points without an intervening sequence point.
questions.explanation: According to the ISO C standard, between the previous and next sequence point a scalar object shall have its stored value modified at most once by the evaluation of an expression. In 'i = (++i) + (i++)', 'i' is modified twice without an intervening sequence point, invoking undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Check the rules regarding modifying a scalar variable more than once between sequence points.
questions.relatedConcept: Undefined behavior from multiple modifications and sequence points
questions.codeSnippet:
int i = 1;
int j = (++i) + (i++);
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test whether a candidate knows the strict limits of expression evaluation rules in C rather than relying on compiler-specific behaviors.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q27] In C99 and later standards, what is the scope and linkage of an identifier declared inside the initialization clause of a 'for' loop?
options: The identifier 'i' has function-wide scope and remains accessible throughout the remainder of the enclosing function.
The identifier 'i' has external linkage and can be accessed by other translation units.
The identifier 'i' has a block scope restricted to the body and condition of the 'for' loop, and cannot be accessed outside.
The identifier 'i' has file scope and persists until the end of the compilation unit.
questions.correctAnswer: The identifier 'i' has a block scope restricted to the body and condition of the 'for' loop, and cannot be accessed outside.
questions.explanation: In C99, a variable declared in the init-clause of a for statement has a scope that encompasses the entire for loop (including the control expression, loop body, and increment expression), acting as if it were declared in a block enclosing the loop. It is not accessible outside the loop.
questions.hint: Think about block scoping introduced in C99 for loop iterators.
questions.relatedConcept: For-loop initialization clause scoping rules
questions.interviewTip: Important for developers transitioning from older C89 standards where loop variables had to be declared at the top of the function.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q28] What is the precise C standard behavior when a signed integer arithmetic operation overflows?
options: Guaranteed wrapping around to INT_MIN in all standard-conforming compilers
Undefined behavior unless compiled with -ftrapv
Automatic promotion to long long to prevent data loss
Undefined behavior according to the ISO C standard
questions.correctAnswer: Undefined behavior according to the ISO C standard
questions.explanation: According to the ISO C standard, signed integer overflow results in undefined behavior. While many compilers wrap around using two's complement arithmetic in practice, the standard allows compilers to assume it never happens for optimization purposes.
questions.hint: Check what the ISO C standard explicitly specifies regarding signed versus unsigned integer types.
questions.relatedConcept: Signed Integer Overflow Undefined Behavior
questions.codeSnippet:
int a = INT_MAX;
int b = a + 1;
questions.interviewTip: Interweaves compiler optimization assumptions with basic data type rules; heavily tested in systems programming interviews.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q29] What is the consequence of modifying a string literal via a non-const pointer in C?
options: Undefined behavior, often resulting in a segmentation fault if stored in read-only memory
Successful modification of the string literal in the data segment
A compile-time error enforced by the C compiler
A guaranteed runtime exception thrown by the C standard library
questions.correctAnswer: Undefined behavior, often resulting in a segmentation fault if stored in read-only memory
questions.explanation: String literals typically reside in read-only data segments of the binary. Attempting to modify them through pointers invokes undefined behavior, which on modern systems triggers a segmentation fault.
questions.hint: Consider where string literals are usually allocated in virtual memory layout.
questions.relatedConcept: String Literal Modifiability
questions.codeSnippet:
char *ptr = "Hello";
ptr[0] = 'h';
questions.interviewTip: Common trap for developers transitioning from C++ or scripting languages where string mutability rules differ.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q30] What is the primary reason why using small arrays with the `alloca()` function can lead to stack overflow vulnerabilities or undefined behavior in C?
options: It allocates memory from the heap that is never garbage collected, causing immediate memory leaks.
It allocates memory directly on the call stack without bounds checks, meaning a large or attacker-controlled size can silently overwrite adjacent stack frames.
It requires a corresponding call to `free()`, which will fault because stack memory cannot be freed explicitly.
It is thread-unsafe and causes race conditions by allocating shared global variables.
questions.correctAnswer: It allocates memory directly on the call stack without bounds checks, meaning a large or attacker-controlled size can silently overwrite adjacent stack frames.
questions.explanation: `alloca()` allocates memory by adjusting the stack pointer dynamically at runtime. Because C provides no built-in mechanism or guard pages to check stack exhaustion against the heap or bounds, an excessively large allocation request will cause a stack overflow, often corrupting return addresses and leading to security vulnerabilities.
questions.hint: Think about where the stack pointer moves and what happens when it collides with other memory regions without guard validation.
questions.relatedConcept: Stack allocation via alloca and memory safety
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of stack versus heap memory management, runtime stack growth, and the security pitfalls of dynamic stack allocation functions like alloca.

questions.question: What is the behavior and result of evaluating the expression 'sizeof(++x)' in C, given an integer variable 'int x = 5;'?
options: sz is the size of int, and x becomes 6 because the compiler evaluates side effects inside the sizeof operand.
sz is the size of int, and x remains 5 because sizeof is evaluated at compile time and its operand is not executed.
The code fails to compile because side effects are explicitly banned inside the sizeof operator by the ISO C standard.
sz is the size of size_t, and x becomes 5 due to immediate cast evaluation rules.
questions.correctAnswer: sz is the size of int, and x remains 5 because sizeof is evaluated at compile time and its operand is not executed.
questions.explanation: According to the ISO C standard, the operand of the 'sizeof' operator is not evaluated (unless it is a VLA whose size is evaluated at runtime). Since 'sizeof' is a compile-time operator for non-VLA types, any side effects (like the pre-increment '++x') inside its operand are completely ignored, leaving 'x' unchanged at 5, and 'sz' equal to 'sizeof(int)'.
questions.hint: Consider whether 'sizeof' is evaluated at compile time or runtime for standard types, and what that implies for expressions with side effects.
questions.relatedConcept: sizeof compile-time evaluation and side effects
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test whether a candidate understands the compile-time nature of the sizeof operator versus runtime execution semantics.

title: C - Test 3: Technical Assessment
description: Dynamic Test 3 for C with 100% unique questions.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q1] A code reviewer flags the following C function as non-idomatic and potentially hazardous in memory-constrained embedded systems. Why is the use of `strdup()` specifically problematic in this context compared to manual `malloc`/`strcpy`?
options: strdup() always allocates memory on the stack, causing immediate stack overflow in nested calls.
strdup() is a non-standard extension not available on all platforms, and it lacks a direct way to check for allocation failure before usage, making it unsafe in strict ISO C environments.
strdup() copies the string twice internally to verify integrity, doubling the time complexity to O(2n).
strdup() implicitly sets the first byte of the new allocation to NULL, corrupting the string structure.
questions.correctAnswer: strdup() is a non-standard extension not available on all platforms, and it lacks a direct way to check for allocation failure before usage, making it unsafe in strict ISO C environments.
questions.explanation: strdup() is an XSI extension (part of POSIX, but not ISO C), and unlike malloc+strcpy, it returns NULL on failure without distinguishing between 'NULL passed in' and 'allocation failed' in some older contexts, though the primary critique in strict embedded/ISO contexts is portability and the implicit chaining of two potentially failing operations into one opaque function call. The other options are technically false: it uses the heap, not stack; it copies once; it does not implicitly null-terminate the first byte incorrectly.
questions.hint: Consider the standard conformance and error handling granularity of library functions.
questions.relatedConcept: Portability and error handling of non-standard string utilities
questions.interviewTip: Tests if a candidate understands the difference between POSIX and ISO C and the importance of explicit error checking in critical systems.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q2] Which of the following C code patterns is most likely to introduce a subtle bug related to signed/unsigned comparison warnings and unexpected behavior in a 32-bit environment when `count` is 0?
options: The loop will never execute because `i` is signed and the limit is unsigned, triggering a compiler error.
The cast `(unsigned int)count` prevents the compiler from optimizing the loop, forcing a runtime check every iteration.
If `get_item_count()` returns -1 (indicating 'no items' or error), casting it to `unsigned int` results in a large positive value, causing an out-of-bounds access or infinite loop.
This pattern is safe because the C standard guarantees that signed integers are converted to unsigned integers by wrapping in a modular arithmetic that prevents overflow.
questions.correctAnswer: If `get_item_count()` returns -1 (indicating 'no items' or error), casting it to `unsigned int` results in a large positive value, causing an out-of-bounds access or infinite loop.
questions.explanation: In C, converting a negative signed integer to an unsigned type is well-defined and results in the corresponding modulo 2^N value. If `count` is -1 (common error/idle code), `(unsigned int)-1` becomes `UINT_MAX` (4294967295). The loop `i < (unsigned int)count` will then iterate until `i` (signed int) overflows or remains negative, leading to undefined behavior or accessing far beyond the array bounds. Option D is wrong because the conversion doesn't 'prevent' overflow; it reinterprets the bits in a way that breaks the loop condition's intent.
questions.hint: Think about what happens if a function returns -1 to indicate 'none' or 'error'.
questions.relatedConcept: Signed/Unsigned conversion pitfalls and implicit type promotion
questions.interviewTip: This reveals if a candidate recognizes the danger of mixing signed and unsigned types in loop conditions, a common source of security vulnerabilities.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q3] What is the behavior and result of using the comma operator in the initialization statement of a standard C `for` loop, such as `for (int i = 0, j = 10; i < j; i++, j--)`?
options: It results in a compile-time syntax error because the comma operator is not permitted inside control statements.
Multiple variables of different types can be declared and initialized in the initialization clause, and multiple expressions can be evaluated in the increment clause.
Only the last expression evaluated via the comma operator determines the loop control variable, rendering 'i' uninitialized.
The loop executes infinitely because the comma operator discards the left-hand side value in all contexts.
questions.correctAnswer: Multiple variables of different types can be declared and initialized in the initialization clause, and multiple expressions can be evaluated in the increment clause.
questions.explanation: In C, the comma operator (and the comma separator in declarations) allows multiple declarations of the same type and multiple independent expressions to be sequenced in the initialization and increment clauses of a `for` loop.
questions.hint: Think about how multiple loop variables are typically set up and updated.
questions.relatedConcept: Comma operator and for-loop syntax rules
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify whether candidates understand the exact sequencing rules and syntax flexibility of C loop constructs.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q4] According to the C standard, what is the precise evaluation order of function arguments when a function is called with multiple expressions containing side effects, such as `func(++a, ++a)`?
options: Strictly left-to-right, ensuring the first argument is always evaluated and incremented before the second argument.
Strictly right-to-left, adhering to standard stack-pushing conventions in calling conventions like cdecl.
Unspecified; the order in which individual arguments and their side effects are evaluated is entirely up to the compiler implementation.
Undefined behavior immediately occurs, causing the compiler to emit a mandatory error.
questions.correctAnswer: Unspecified; the order in which individual arguments and their side effects are evaluated is entirely up to the compiler implementation.
questions.explanation: The C standard specifies that the order of evaluation of the function designator, the actual arguments, and their sub-expressions are unspecified. Relying on side effects among function arguments leads to non-portable and unpredictable code.
questions.hint: Consider whether C guarantees argument evaluation order like Java or C# do.
questions.relatedConcept: Unspecified evaluation order and sequence points
questions.interviewTip: This is a classic systems programming trap question that exposes whether a candidate relies on dangerous undefined or unspecified compiler behaviors.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q5] What is the standard-defined behavior in C when executing compound assignment or increment/decrement operators on a scalar object without an intervening sequence point?
options: Deterministic behavior returning 11
Deterministic behavior returning 10
Guaranteed left-to-right evaluation resulting in 12
Undefined behavior
questions.correctAnswer: Undefined behavior
questions.explanation: According to the C standard (ISO/IEC 9899), between previous and next sequence points a scalar object shall have its stored value modified at most once by the evaluation of an expression. Furthermore, the prior value shall be read only to determine the value to be stored. Expressions like 'i++ + i++' violate these rules, resulting in undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Check the C standard rules regarding modification of a scalar object multiple times between sequence points.
questions.relatedConcept: Sequence points and undefined behavior in expression evaluation
questions.codeSnippet:
int i = 5;
int j = i++ + i++;
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test whether candidates understand the limits of expression evaluation order and the dangerous pitfalls of modifying the same variable multiple times in a single statement.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q6] What is the primary reason why calling `longjmp()` across thread boundaries or after the function that invoked `setjmp()` has returned is strictly forbidden?
options: The stack frame containing the setjmp invocation has been destroyed and returning to it corrupts the execution context.
It causes an immediate kernel-level deadlock.
It forces the compiler to disable all optimizations globally.
It only causes a memory leak of the jmp_buf structure.
questions.correctAnswer: The stack frame containing the setjmp invocation has been destroyed and returning to it corrupts the execution context.
questions.explanation: When a function returns, its stack frame is popped and becomes invalid. Invoking longjmp() to restore an environment whose stack frame no longer exists results in undefined behavior because the stack pointer and frame pointers would point to reclaimed or reused stack space.
questions.hint: Think about the lifecycle of stack frames during function returns.
questions.relatedConcept: Lifecycle of stack frames and non-local jumps via setjmp/longjmp
questions.interviewTip: This tests deep knowledge of C runtime stack management and control flow redirection functions.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q7] What is the primary compliance risk when using standard library functions like `strtok()` in a multi-threaded C application without locking mechanisms?
options: strtok() allocates temporary memory dynamically using malloc(), which causes thread-safety issues in the heap allocator.
strtok() uses a hidden internal static buffer to track parsing state across calls, leading to race conditions and data corruption.
strtok() modifies the original string in-place, which is forbidden across thread boundaries regardless of synchronization.
strtok() blocks thread execution globally by acquiring an exclusive lock on the standard input stream.
questions.correctAnswer: strtok() uses a hidden internal static buffer to track parsing state across calls, leading to race conditions and data corruption.
questions.explanation: The POSIX standard `strtok()` function relies on an internal static pointer to keep track of the string being parsed between subsequent calls where the first argument is NULL. This makes it inherently non-reentrant and thread-unsafe, as concurrent threads would overwrite each other's parsing state.
questions.hint: Think about how strtok remembers where it left off when you pass NULL as its first argument.
questions.relatedConcept: Thread safety and reentrancy of standard library functions like strtok
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers test this to check if you know when to prefer thread-safe alternatives like strtok_r().

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q8] Consider an expression involving signed and unsigned integer promotion in C. What is the execution behavior when comparing a negative signed integer to a larger unsigned integer of the same conversion rank (e.g., int vs unsigned int)?
options: The unsigned integer 'u' is converted to a signed integer, preserving its value, making the comparison (s < u) evaluate to true.
The comparison results in undefined behavior according to the C standard.
The signed integer 's' is converted to an unsigned integer, wrapping around to a very large positive number, making the comparison (s < u) evaluate to false.
The compiler issues a compilation error due to type mismatch in relational comparisons.
questions.correctAnswer: The signed integer 's' is converted to an unsigned integer, wrapping around to a very large positive number, making the comparison (s < u) evaluate to false.
questions.explanation: According to C's usual arithmetic conversions, when operands of equal rank are signed and unsigned, the signed operand is converted to the unsigned type. Thus, -5 converts to UINT_MAX - 4, which is much larger than 10, causing the condition to be false.
questions.hint: Remember the C conversion rule: when mixing signed and unsigned of the same width, the signed value becomes unsigned.
questions.relatedConcept: Usual arithmetic conversions and signed-to-unsigned comparison pitfalls
questions.interviewTip: This is a classic systems-programming interview question used to catch subtle bugs in boundary checks.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q9] What is the primary danger of using `strncpy(dest, src, sizeof(dest));` when `src` is equal to or longer than `sizeof(dest)`?
options: The function will automatically trigger a segmentation fault upon encountering the buffer limit.
The function will throw a compile-time warning or error due to buffer overflow violation.
The destination buffer will be safely null-terminated at the last byte, truncating the string gracefully.
The destination buffer will not be null-terminated, potentially leading to buffer over-reads in subsequent string operations.
questions.correctAnswer: The destination buffer will not be null-terminated, potentially leading to buffer over-reads in subsequent string operations.
questions.explanation: strncpy does not guarantee null-termination if the source string length is greater than or equal to the specified size limit. If dest is filled completely without a null character, subsequent standard string functions like strlen or printf will read past the end of dest, causing undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the trailing null character when the source string completely fills or exceeds the size argument.
questions.relatedConcept: String utility pitfalls and lack of guaranteed null-termination in strncpy
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if developers understand the subtle safety traps of legacy string manipulation functions.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q10] What is the specific C standard behavior when performing a bitwise shift left (`<<`) on a signed integer where the operand is positive but the result overflows the width of the target type's signed representation?
options: It results in undefined behavior according to the C standard.
It is guaranteed to wrap around modulo 2^n in modern compilers.
It invokes arithmetic right shift implementation-defined conversion.
It automatically promotes the result to a signed long long type.
questions.correctAnswer: It results in undefined behavior according to the C standard.
questions.explanation: According to the ISO C standard, shifting a signed integer left by a count greater than or equal to the width of the type, or shifting a value where the resulting mathematical value cannot be represented in the result type (signed overflow), results in undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Check how the C standard classifies signed integer overflow across bitwise operations.
questions.relatedConcept: Signed integer overflow behavior during bitwise shift operations
questions.interviewTip: This question screens for deep knowledge of the C standard versus common compiler behaviors regarding integer representation and safety.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q11] What is the standard compliance behavior regarding stream buffering when stdout is redirected to a file rather than an interactive terminal?
options: stdout becomes unbuffered to ensure all logs are written immediately
stdout switches from line-buffered or unbuffered to fully buffered mode
stdout retains its original interactive terminal buffering mode
The standard library automatically disables buffering for all streams
questions.correctAnswer: stdout switches from line-buffered or unbuffered to fully buffered mode
questions.explanation: According to the C standard, when a stream is determined not to refer to an interactive device (such as when redirected to a file), it is fully buffered. Interactive streams like terminals are typically line-buffered.
questions.hint: Think about how block sizes and performance optimization differ between writing to a disk file versus a terminal screen.
questions.relatedConcept: Stream buffering behavior and terminal detection
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test deep knowledge of standard I/O implementation details beyond basic printf usage.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q12] What is the lifecycle and linkage behavior of a local variable declared with the 'static' specifier inside a function?
options: It has static storage duration and block scope with internal linkage
It has automatic storage duration and block scope with external linkage
It has static storage duration and block scope with no linkage
It has thread storage duration and global scope with no linkage
questions.correctAnswer: It has static storage duration and block scope with no linkage
questions.explanation: A local static variable retains its value between function calls (static storage duration) and is only visible within the block it is declared in (block scope with no linkage).
questions.hint: Consider where the variable can be accessed from outside the function and how long it lives.
questions.relatedConcept: Storage duration, scope, and linkage of static variables
questions.interviewTip: Crucial for embedded and systems programming where persistent local state is required without polluting global namespace.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q13] What is the behavior regarding sequence points and side effects in the C expression `x = i++ + i++;` where `i` is initialized to 1?
options: The expression guarantees left-to-right evaluation, resulting in x = 1 + 2 = 3, and i becomes 3.
The expression guarantees right-to-left evaluation, resulting in x = 2 + 1 = 3, and i becomes 3.
The behavior is fully defined in C99 and later standards, evaluating to x = 4 and i = 3.
The behavior is undefined due to multiple unsequenced modifications of the same object 'i' within the same expression.
questions.correctAnswer: The behavior is undefined due to multiple unsequenced modifications of the same object 'i' within the same expression.
questions.explanation: According to the C standard, between the previous and next sequence point (or execution of a full expression), an object's stored value shall be modified at most once by the evaluation of an expression. In 'i++ + i++', 'i' is modified twice without an intervening sequence point, invoking undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Check the C standard rules regarding modifying a variable multiple times without an intervening sequence point.
questions.relatedConcept: Undefined behavior from unsequenced side effects on scalar objects
questions.codeSnippet:
int i = 1;
int x = i++ + i++;
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify a candidate's understanding of undefined behavior regarding side effects and operator precedence.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q14] In C, what is the exact execution behavior of the comma operator in the expression `int x = (a = 3, b = 5, a + b);`?
options: The expressions are evaluated from left to right, a sequence point occurs after each comma, and x receives the value of the rightmost subexpression (8).
All three subexpressions are evaluated concurrently; x receives an indeterminate value.
Only the rightmost subexpression 'a + b' is evaluated, meaning 'a' and 'b' remain uninitialized.
The comma operator acts as a list initializer, causing a compilation error in standard C.
questions.correctAnswer: The expressions are evaluated from left to right, a sequence point occurs after each comma, and x receives the value of the rightmost subexpression (8).
questions.explanation: The comma operator (,) guarantees that its operands are evaluated sequentially from left to right. There is a sequence point after the evaluation of the first operand, and the value and type of the result of the whole comma expression are the value and type of the rightmost operand.
questions.hint: Recall that the comma operator introduces a strict sequencing order and yields the value of its final operand.
questions.relatedConcept: The comma operator and evaluation sequencing
questions.codeSnippet:
int a, b;
int x = (a = 3, b = 5, a + b);
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers test this to see if candidates know that the comma operator is more than just a separator in function arguments.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q15] What does a sudden SIGSEGV (Segmentation Fault) occurring specifically inside a library function (e.g., `memcpy` or `strcpy`) typically imply about the caller's responsibility?
options: The operating system has run out of physical swap space, terminating the process.
The source or destination pointer provided by the caller is invalid, unaligned for vector instructions, or points to out-of-bounds memory.
The linked library version is incompatible with the CPU architecture's instruction set.
The compiler optimized away the stack frame pointer, violating the calling convention.
questions.correctAnswer: The source or destination pointer provided by the caller is invalid, unaligned for vector instructions, or points to out-of-bounds memory.
questions.explanation: High-performance library implementations like `memcpy` often utilize optimized vector instructions (e.g., SIMD/AVX). If the caller passes a wild pointer, an unmapped address, or memory lacking proper alignment, the hardware instruction triggers a segmentation fault directly inside the routine.
questions.hint: Think about what high-speed memory routines assume about the pointers passed to them.
questions.relatedConcept: SIGSEGV symptoms in standard library routines
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if a candidate distinguishes between bugs in standard library internals versus incorrect API usage by the caller.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q16] An embedded C program intermittently hangs or locks up completely without crashing or triggering any exception handler. Which diagnostic symptom strongly points toward a missing volatile qualifier?
options: The hardware watchdog timer expired because the program execution took longer than expected.
A stack overflow occurred due to deep recursion inside an interrupt service routine.
The compiler optimized the polling loop into an infinite check of a cached register value, ignoring external hardware updates.
Dynamic memory fragmentation caused an unrecoverable out-of-memory deadlock.
questions.correctAnswer: The compiler optimized the polling loop into an infinite check of a cached register value, ignoring external hardware updates.
questions.explanation: Without `volatile`, the compiler assumes no external entity changes `status_register` during the loop, so it reads the variable into a CPU register once and loops infinitely on that cached value, missing hardware updates.
questions.hint: Consider how optimizers handle variables that do not change within the local execution thread.
questions.relatedConcept: volatile keyword and compiler optimization symptom
questions.codeSnippet: while (status_register == 0); // Polling loop
questions.interviewTip: This question assesses whether the candidate understands the exact runtime symptom of a missing `volatile` keyword in hardware-facing code.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q17] What is the standard-defined behavior when calling 'strncat()' where the destination buffer size 'n' (the third parameter) is smaller than or equal to the actual string length of the source string?
options: It triggers a buffer overflow if the combined length exceeds the total size of the destination array regardless of 'n'.
It copies exactly 2 bytes without appending a null terminator, leaving the destination string unterminated.
It fails to compile or returns an error code because 'n' must be greater than the source string length.
It appends at most 2 characters from the source, explicitly writes a terminating null byte at the end of the appended characters, and guarantees the resulting destination string is null-terminated.
questions.correctAnswer: It appends at most 2 characters from the source, explicitly writes a terminating null byte at the end of the appended characters, and guarantees the resulting destination string is null-terminated.
questions.explanation: Unlike 'strncpy', 'strncat' always guarantees null-termination of the destination string. It appends at most 'n' characters from the source and then appends a terminating null byte ('\0') automatically.
questions.hint: Think about how 'strncat' differs from 'strncpy' regarding safety and mandatory null-termination.
questions.relatedConcept: Safe string manipulation and library contract boundaries in C
questions.codeSnippet:
char dest[10] = "Hello";
strncat(dest, "World", 2);
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers often test 'strncat' to see if candidates understand that 'n' specifies the maximum source bytes to append, distinct from the total destination buffer capacity.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q18] What is the behavior of the standard library function 'sscanf()' when encountering an input stream that does not match the expected format specifier?
options: It returns 0, and the variable 'val' retains its original value (42).
It returns EOF, and the variable 'val' is overwritten with zero.
It triggers a runtime segmentation fault due to type mismatch.
It returns -1, and 'val' becomes undefined.
questions.correctAnswer: It returns 0, and the variable 'val' retains its original value (42).
questions.explanation: If no items are successfully matched and assigned, 'sscanf()' returns 0. Variables corresponding to unsatisfied conversion specifiers are left unchanged.
questions.hint: Examine the return value convention of matching functions when parsing fails immediately.
questions.relatedConcept: Formatted input parsing return codes and side-effects
questions.codeSnippet:
int val = 42;
int ret = sscanf("abc", "%d", &val);
questions.interviewTip: Useful for assessing robust error handling when parsing untrusted string inputs.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q19] According to the ISO C standard, what is the exact behavior when a signed integer operation results in a value that cannot be represented in the destination type (overflow)?
options: It wraps around using two's complement arithmetic, guaranteed across all conformant implementations.
It is undefined behavior, meaning the compiler can assume it never happens and optimize accordingly.
It is trapped automatically by the hardware, generating a SIGFPE signal on all platforms.
It saturates at the maximum or minimum representable value of the integer type.
questions.correctAnswer: It is undefined behavior, meaning the compiler can assume it never happens and optimize accordingly.
questions.explanation: The C standard explicitly defines signed integer overflow as undefined behavior, whereas unsigned integer overflow is well-defined and wraps around modulo 2^n. Compilers rely on this undefined behavior for optimizations like loop invariant code motion.
questions.hint: Think about what the C standard says regarding signed vs. unsigned arithmetic boundaries.
questions.relatedConcept: Signed Integer Overflow Undefined Behavior
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers check this to see if candidates confuse C's handling of signed integers with Java or hardware-level two's complement guarantees.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q20] What is the primary portability limitation and safety risk associated with using the standard library function `strtok()` in multithreaded environments?
options: It automatically frees the input string pointer, causing double-free issues if called from multiple threads.
It allocates memory internally using `malloc()`, leading to thread synchronization locks and severe heap fragmentation.
It maintains an internal static state across calls for a given string, making it non-reentrant and not thread-safe.
It enforces a strict null-termination check that crashes if the input string is modified concurrently.
questions.correctAnswer: It maintains an internal static state across calls for a given string, making it non-reentrant and not thread-safe.
questions.explanation: `strtok()` uses a hidden internal static pointer to keep track of the remaining string during tokenization. Consequently, concurrent calls from multiple threads cause data races and corrupted parsing. The reentrant counterpart `strtok_r()` should be used instead.
questions.hint: Consider how `strtok` remembers where it left off between successive calls with a NULL first argument.
questions.relatedConcept: Non-reentrant functions and thread safety of strtok
questions.interviewTip: Frequently asked in systems programming to assess knowledge of thread-safe APIs and reentrancy versus thread-safety.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q21] What is the primary danger of using standard library functions like `printf` or `malloc` inside a POSIX signal handler?
options: They automatically disable all other pending signals on the system, leading to dropped interrupt notifications.
They cause an immediate segmentation fault because signal handlers lack access to the process text segment.
They will always trigger a compiler warning that aborts the build process.
These functions are generally not async-signal-safe and can cause undefined behavior, deadlocks, or heap corruption if they interrupt a routine that was already executing them.
questions.correctAnswer: These functions are generally not async-signal-safe and can cause undefined behavior, deadlocks, or heap corruption if they interrupt a routine that was already executing them.
questions.explanation: Many standard library functions maintain internal global state or use non-reentrant locks (such as heap management locks or stream buffers). If a signal arrives and interrupts a thread already inside `malloc` or `printf`, and the signal handler calls the same function, the internal state can become corrupted or cause a deadlock.
questions.hint: Think about reentrancy and shared global state in runtime libraries.
questions.relatedConcept: Async-signal-safety in C signal handlers
questions.interviewTip: This tests systems-level C knowledge and defensive programming around asynchronous events.

questions.question: [C • Test 3 • Q22] What is the behavior of the `assert()` macro when the preprocessor identifier `NDEBUG` is defined prior to including `<assert.h>`?
options: The `assert()` macro expands to nothing, effectively disabling runtime evaluation of the assertion condition.
The `assert()` expression is completely evaluated at compile-time and throws a compiler error if `x` is unknown.
The assertion is converted into a static_assert checked by the compiler.
The program terminates immediately at startup if `NDEBUG` is defined.
questions.correctAnswer: The `assert()` macro expands to nothing, effectively disabling runtime evaluation of the assertion condition.
questions.explanation: According to the ISO C standard, if `NDEBUG` is defined at the moment `<assert.h>` is included, the `assert()` macro is defined simply as `((void)0)`, completely removing the check and its expression from the compiled code.
questions.hint: Check the C standard definition regarding diagnostic macros and release builds.
